So far in 2026 downloads of standalone delivery apps in America and Canada are down by a fifth from the same period a year before, estimates Sensor Tower, a market-intelligence firm.

Today consolidation is in order. On October 29th DoorDash, a meal-delivery firm, said it would buy Instacart, a competitor focused on groceries, for $17bn. DoorDash expects the merger will eventually yield $500m of extra profit a year as the two firms fuse their software systems and advertising arms. If the merged entity is to take on Amazon and Walmart, which within a few years have come to dominate America’s online-grocery market, it will need every penny.

Online sales now account for a fifth of Americans’ spending on groceries, according to Brick Meets Click, a data provider. They have grown by more than 20% year on year for eight quarters. Yet the boom has benefited retail behemoths more than gig-economy disrupters. Walmart learned to be a tech firm and Amazon a grocer faster than newcomers could gain a foothold.

The two giants now account for 55% of America’s online-grocery sales, reckons Wedbush, a financial-services firm. Their expansion has squeezed Instacart and DoorDash, as well as others such as Uber Eats and Grubhub. Lately the upstarts have had to rely more on paid referrals and ads to win customers. “Everybody is fighting for the scraps left after the top players,” says Aaron Cheris of Bain, a consultancy.

In search of scale and new markets, delivery apps worldwide have been on a shopping spree. Last year DoorDash snapped up Britain’s Deliveroo just as Prosus, a technology-investment firm that owns delivery apps around the world, bought Just Eat Takeaway, a Dutch rival. Uber is poised to snaffle Delivery Hero, based in Berlin; it also considered gobbling up Instacart at least twice.

DoorDash’s purchase of Instacart, however, is about expanding within America. It will help DoorDash move further into groceries, which need more complex software than takeaway meals because workers have to shop in-store and find substitutes for missing items rather than just waiting for a brown-bagged restaurant order. It also allows DoorDash to combine Instacart’s ad business, which enjoys enviably high margins, with its own. For Instacart the deal offers the protection of scale: DoorDash’s market value of $73bn is more than five times its own.

Even under the deal-loving Trump administration, the merger is not sure to go through. As the midterm elections have shown, “affordability” is the hottest of political topics. Regulators may frown on deals that they suspect will push grocery bills up. Last month DoorDash and Instacart (as well as Uber and Walmart) were among the firms from which the Federal Trade Commission, a competition regulator, requested information on their use of personalised pricing.

DoorDash and Instacart argue that greater scale will mean lower costs and hence cheaper groceries. What is more, they add that their combined platform will help corner shops fend off the grocery giants. DoorDash has gone so far as to roll out a website called Shop Local Together, replete with mentions of affordability.

Even if regulators can be convinced of the merits of a deal, the combined business will be far from a guaranteed success. A combined DoorDash and Instacart should outmatch its gig-economy peers. But to thrive it will have to stand up to the world’s biggest retailers. That is a much harder sell. ■

item.title: 好奇心是否被神化了？
item.description:
Business

商业 | 巴特比 2026年11月5日 在任何关于未来人工智能影响下雇主看重的人类品质的讨论中，总有几个特质反复出现：品味、判断力、同理心、专业能力。这些“宾果卡”词汇中有一个是好奇心。支持者认为，好奇心强的人更可能探索新技术的轮廓，掌握新技能。如果你想要一支能够适应快速变化的员工队伍，求知欲就是一种超能力。 几乎不可能反对好奇心——这也解释了为什么求职者不会吹嘘自己对周围世界完全没兴趣。但当所有人都同意某件事时，通常值得思考是否还有另一面。 诚然，好奇心有很多好处。约克大学的苏菲·冯·斯图姆及其合著者的一项元分析表明，求知欲可以预测学业成功。好奇心有助于学习。卡迪夫大学的马蒂亚斯·格鲁伯及...
item.content:encoded:
好奇心是否被神化了？

商业 | 巴特比 2026年11月5日

在任何关于未来人工智能影响下雇主看重的人类品质的讨论中，总有几个特质反复出现：品味、判断力、同理心、专业能力。这些“宾果卡”词汇中有一个是好奇心。支持者认为，好奇心强的人更可能探索新技术的轮廓，掌握新技能。如果你想要一支能够适应快速变化的员工队伍，求知欲就是一种超能力。

几乎不可能反对好奇心——这也解释了为什么求职者不会吹嘘自己对周围世界完全没兴趣。但当所有人都同意某件事时，通常值得思考是否还有另一面。

诚然，好奇心有很多好处。约克大学的苏菲·冯·斯图姆及其合著者的一项元分析表明，求知欲可以预测学业成功。好奇心有助于学习。卡迪夫大学的马蒂亚斯·格鲁伯及其同事的一项研究发现，人们对那些急切想要了解的信息（甚至是在好奇心高涨时偶然学到的东西）有更好的记忆。好奇心也有助于创造力。在阿卡迈科技的莉迪亚·潘恩·哈格特维特及其合著者的一篇论文中，参与者被要求猜测哈利·胡迪尼是如何表演让大象消失的幻术的。那些被告知“答案接近但不正确”的人，在后续想出新把戏的挑战中，比被告知“猜对了”的对照组表现更好。解谜的渴望是让人们探索各种不同想法的有效方式。

同样的渴望还能以其他方式使组织受益。好奇心能勾起消费者的兴趣。升级到LinkedIn高级版一定还有更好的理由，但没有什么比想知道到底是谁一直在看你的个人资料更有说服力了。如果慈善募捐者索要非常规的金额，而不是通常的整数（比如8.23美元而不是10美元），人们似乎更有可能捐款。请求的具体性激发了兴趣，打断了那些“我还有个会要开”的排练好的说辞。神秘感也可以用来筛选好奇的求职者。谷歌曾把一道数学题贴在广告牌上，而没有透露出题者正是自己。任何感兴趣到去解题的人都会被引导到一个招聘网站。

尽管如此，“好奇的员工必然对组织完全有益”的直觉仍值得质疑。一方面，好奇心本质上会分散注意力。例如，本专栏的前两段中包含了英语中最长的单词之一，其字母按字母顺序排列；一个非常好奇的人现在就会开始寻找它，而不是继续往下读。爱追根究底的同事会拉扯线头，问越来越多的问题，要求越来越多的数据。他们可能会发现一些有价值的东西，也可能只是拖延了决策。欧洲工商管理学院的斯宾塞·哈里森解释说，好奇心意味着从你当前的焦点转移到吸引你注意力的其他事物上。他是一篇关于“生产性低效”的论文的合著者，该论文探讨了短期绕道如何带来潜在的长期回报。

好奇心还与自主性密切相关。新英格兰大学的尼古拉·舒特和约翰·马洛夫的一项研究让参与者观看视频。那些可以自主选择看什么的人，比那些被指定看什么的人对视频主题更感兴趣。这给组织提出了一个问题：员工在探索自己感兴趣的问题时应该有多少自由空间。

在《科学思维模式》这本新书中，哈佛商学院的斯特凡·汤姆克描述了Booking.com的实验文化。这家旅游网站以允许产品团队自行对新功能进行A/B测试而闻名，任何时刻大约有1000个测试在并行进行。这种去中心化对许多公司来说将是一个飞跃。

一个雇佣好奇员工的组织，总是比一个选择目光呆滞之人的组织要好。但充分利用好奇心意味着接受权衡——花在死胡同里的时间，大部分在视线之外进行的实验。好奇心几乎没有什么坏处。几乎。■

欢迎通过我们的巴特比通讯走进职场世界。每周，我们的白领智者都会思考办公室生活的种种痛苦。

item.title: America’s copper giant has big dreams—but cautious plans
item.description:
Business

Business | Scratching the surface Nov 5th 2026 Among the few areas of bipartisan consensus in Washington these days is the belief that securing access to critical minerals is vital to the national interest. In many cases Chinese miners have already established a daunting lead. But not in copper....
item.content:encoded:
America’s copper giant has big dreams—but cautious plans

Business | Scratching the surface

Nov 5th 2026

Among the few areas of bipartisan consensus in Washington these days is the belief that securing access to critical minerals is vital to the national interest. In many cases Chinese miners have already established a daunting lead. But not in copper. That is thanks in no small part to Freeport-McMoRan, an American miner that is the world’s second biggest producer of the red metal, after BHP, a diversified Australian giant (see chart 1).

“Today really is Freeport’s time,” says Kathleen Quirk, chief executive of the Phoenix-based miner. Electrification and the artificial-intelligence boom will keep lifting copper demand, she argues, yet new supply is scarce and slow to develop. In the past 15 months copper prices have surged by 40%, bringing Freeport’s share price with them (see chart 2). That, combined with new technology and greater political support, leads Ms Quirk to suggest that America may be on the cusp of a copper version of the shale revolution. People once assumed that the country would remain dependent on imported oil and gas; instead it became a major exporter. Ms Quirk reckons her industry could see something similar.

One day, perhaps. But the strategy now being pursued by America’s copper giant will contribute only modestly. Last month Freeport said it was aiming to lift its total output of the metal to 4.5bn-5bn pounds by 2030, up from a projected 3bn in 2026. Its approach is strikingly incremental.

Freeport’s first priority is to restore output at its biggest mine—Grasberg, in Indonesia, which usually accounts for over 35% of its output (and is 51% owned by the Indonesian government). Since a giant mudslide in 2025 that killed seven workers, production there has been below par. Ms Quirk expects the site to have fully recovered by the end of 2027.

Next is to selectively expand existing sites. Most advanced is a plan to double the capacity of Bagdad, an 81-year-old mine in Arizona. On November 4th Freeport said its board had approved the $4.5bn investment, which Will Tankard of CRU, a consultancy, describes as “low risk”. Freeport says the project, which has all its permits, will break even at $4 a pound; copper trades near $6.40 today.

Bagdad’s doubling could add up to 250m pounds a year of copper supply by 2030. Freeport is also studying another mine expansion in Arizona, and seeking permits for one at El Abra in Chile, though neither will start before the next decade.

The final focus for Freeport is on new technology. At most of its mines it deposits ores that contain too little copper into giant stockpiles. These now hold about 40bn pounds of copper, says Ms Quirk.

To extract more from that ore, Freeport is experimenting with new forms of “leaching”, which uses acid to dissolve copper from rock. Last month the miner said it had tested a solution in the lab that may let it recover 800m pounds of copper a year from the stockpiles by 2030, up from a current annualised rate of 220m. Trials are planned in the field next year.

In 2025 Freeport has also converted Bagdad’s fleet to autonomous trucks. Ms Quirk says it plans to do the same elsewhere in America within the next few years to ease labour constraints, allowing it to produce more from existing mines. The company recently opened a centre in Phoenix to remotely perform dispatch work that used to be done on site.

For investors, however, Freeport has recently lost some of its lustre. From a peak in August, its share price has fallen by more than 20%. Partly that reflects disappointment over a downward revision to its projected sales and an upward revision to its capital expenditure over the near term. But it also points to discontent over the miner’s cautious approach.

Freeport has signalled little appetite for big acquisitions. Its strategy also lacks the “greenfield” projects that would be needed to vastly expand output—and turn America into a global copper power. That may reflect uncertainty over whether copper prices will continue to surge. A slowing global economy and the stagnation in China’s property market are weighing on demand. Tom Price of Panmure Liberum, a broker, reckons that this year’s price rally was caused mostly by hedge funds treating copper futures as a proxy for AI investment. If the data-centre binge comes to a halt, Freeport’s restraint will prove wise. ■

item.title: CVS的分拆标志着美国医疗保健的转折点
item.description:
Business

商业 | 疲惫不堪 2026年11月5日 上世纪60年代，马萨诸塞州的两兄弟共同创立了一家名为“消费者价值商店”的连锁药店。如今，CVS已是美国最大的此类企业。然而，随着时间推移，它早已不仅是一家药店——先是扩展到与制药商谈判批量折扣这一蓬勃发展的业务，继而推出自己的医疗保险计划。在这三个市场中，它都是美国最大的公司之一（见图表）。11月4日，CVS宣布将拆分为两家公司，从而解除这种垂直整合模式。一半将主要由其保险部门和负责谈判药价的药品福利管理公司（PBM）组成，年收入约为3000亿美元。另一半则将囊括其零售药房和免预约诊所，两者合计年销售额略超900亿美元。按受影响的收入衡量，这是十多年...
item.content:encoded:
CVS的分拆标志着美国医疗保健的转折点

商业 | 疲惫不堪 2026年11月5日

上世纪60年代，马萨诸塞州的两兄弟共同创立了一家名为“消费者价值商店”的连锁药店。如今，CVS已是美国最大的此类企业。然而，随着时间推移，它早已不仅是一家药店——先是扩展到与制药商谈判批量折扣这一蓬勃发展的业务，继而推出自己的医疗保险计划。在这三个市场中，它都是美国最大的公司之一（见图表）。11月4日，CVS宣布将拆分为两家公司，从而解除这种垂直整合模式。一半将主要由其保险部门和负责谈判药价的药品福利管理公司（PBM）组成，年收入约为3000亿美元。另一半则将囊括其零售药房和免预约诊所，两者合计年销售额略超900亿美元。按受影响的收入衡量，这是十多年来最大规模的分拆，也是医疗保健行业有史以来最大的一次。这同时标志着该行业的一个转折点。

当CVS在2018年收购医疗保险公司安泰时，它称赞这笔交易是美国医疗保健新模式的开始。通过整合并控制美国错综复杂的医疗体系中的大部分环节，企业将变得更高效。有时，保险部门一直是痛苦之源；两年前，由于公司误判了其健康计划患者的服务成本，利润曾大幅下滑。但自那以后，CVS的老板戴维·乔伊纳使安泰恢复了健康——并证明了垂直整合模式的盈利能力。那么，为何要放弃它？答案可能在于日益敌对的政治环境。美国立法者——无论是共和党还是民主党——都开始批评垂直整合的医疗保健公司，指责它们将高成本转嫁给消费者。批评者尤其关注药店与PBM之间的联盟。与PBM合并使连锁药店得以分享这些中间商从制药公司那里收取的、往往不透明的返利分成，并将更多业务导向自家门店。政客们现在谴责这种做法是反竞争的。2025年，阿肯色州成为第一个通过法律禁止药店与PBM整合的州，尽管该法律因CVS等公司提出挑战而在法庭上受阻。南加州大学的尼拉杰·苏德认为，其他州很快就会效仿。田纳西州已经这样做了。

投资者似乎对分拆计划感到紧张。消息公布后，CVS股价下跌了13%。这可能反映出分拆后零售部门的黯淡前景。CVS的药房业务是市场领导者，表现优于沃尔格林等竞争对手——后者已于2025年被私有化。但摩根大通银行的分析师估计，调整后营业利润率已从2021年的7.1%降至今年的4.7%。威胁比比皆是。礼来和诺和诺德等制药商正通过直接向消费者销售减肥针和其他药物来绕过药店。包括亚马逊在内的电商公司也在进军药店业务。此外，即使是CVS的保险与福利部门，也可能很快成为政客们的靶子。“如果每家保险公司都有自己的PBM，新PBM就没有进入市场的动力，”苏德博士说，因为许多潜在客户已经被抢占了。美国医疗保健领域垂直整合的终结或许才刚刚开始。■

item.title: The quest for immortality has become serious business
item.description:
Business

Business | Forever bound Nov 5th 2026 On a quiet street in the posh London neighbourhood of Chelsea resides HUM2N, a longevity clinic. Inside, a man in socks, gloves and a headband steps into a fridge-sized cabinet chilled to -110°C. A few minutes of “cryotherapy” leave him, by his own account, ...
item.content:encoded:
The quest for immortality has become serious business

Business | Forever bound

Nov 5th 2026

On a quiet street in the posh London neighbourhood of Chelsea resides HUM2N, a longevity clinic. Inside, a man in socks, gloves and a headband steps into a fridge-sized cabinet chilled to -110°C. A few minutes of “cryotherapy” leave him, by his own account, invigorated. Next door a woman lies in a hyperbaric chamber—a pressurised capsule resembling a small submarine—breathing pure oxygen. Other clients take intravenous drips of NAD+, a molecule that cells need to turn food into energy; or have their blood drawn, mixed with ozone and put back. A package of five sessions at the clinic costs £3,000 ($4,025).

The quest to live for ever has lately garnered new interest. Dario Amodei, boss of Anthropic, an artificial-intelligence lab, has suggested that his technology could raise the human lifespan to 150 years. Sam Altman, his counterpart at OpenAI, has put more than $180m into Retro Biosciences, a startup aiming to add ten healthy years to human life. The powerful beyond Silicon Valley are eager, too. Last year Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin were overheard musing that organ transplants might one day make immortality possible.

HUM2N’s clients range from bosses to athletes to patients in their 80s with chronic disease, says Mohammed Enayat, its founder. As the world ages, interest in living longer is seeping into the mainstream. Across the OECD, a club of mostly rich countries, nearly a fifth of people are aged 65 or over; by 2050 more than a quarter will be. One of the loudest evangelists is Bryan Johnson, a tech entrepreneur who hopes never to die. He has turned his regime into a Netflix documentary and a YouTube channel with more than 2m subscribers.

Two very different industries are looking to seize on the opportunity. The first is a colourful and lightly regulated group of clinics and online businesses selling supplements, scans and treatments of sometimes dubious efficacy. The second is slower moving but more consequential. Working in concert with the world’s biggest drugmakers, a crop of biotechs is developing medicines that might slow ageing itself—or even reverse it.

The prize is enormous. Pharma bosses long dismissed obesity as a niche market. GLP-1s proved them wrong, and made Eli Lilly the first drugmaker worth $1trn. A medicine that slowed ageing could be bigger still. “You can sell one year of life,” muses Alex Zhavoronkov, the founder of Insilico Medicine, an AI drug-discovery firm. “How much can you charge?”

Such a drug may be years away, if it comes at all. Into the gap has rushed a business catering to the impatient, one that sits largely outside conventional health care. Insurers cover almost none of it, so customers pay in cash.

First comes measurement, on the belief that tracking everything will catch problems early enough to fix them. Providers offer blood tests, genome sequencing and full-body scans that promise to spot cancers or autoimmune disorders before symptoms appear. Prenuvo, one such firm, charges around $4,000 for an MRI scan of a patient’s entire body. Many sell annual subscriptions, retesting customers regularly to look for changes. Neko Health, a Swedish provider backed by Daniel Ek, a co-founder of Spotify, raised $700m in July ahead of its launch in America.

Next comes treatment. Much of that takes place in longevity clinics like HUM2N. Some estimates put the number of these at about 800 in America alone. The label is unregulated and vague, says Andrea Maier of the National University of Singapore, who co-founded a longevity clinic herself. At too many, she says, customers pick their own treatment, as though ordering pizza. “It’s not care.”

The most adventurous patients head to Roatán, an island off Honduras, where clinics offer gene therapy, stem-cell infusions and other experimental treatments. Others turn to social media, where a growing number of influencers peddle elixirs. Mr Johnson’s company, Blueprint, sells supplements, a powdered “longevity mix”—and olive oil. Then there are the many online businesses selling injectable “peptides”, including the “Wolverine stack”, a combination that is claimed to speed the repair of muscles and tendons.

Little of this rests on solid science. The American College of Radiology, a professional body, says there is “no documented evidence” that full-body screening is cost-effective or prolongs life. Such scans can lead to over-diagnosis, turning up harmless anomalies that prompt needless further tests. The treatments fare no better. Studies of NAD+ supplements have been inconclusive or shown limited effect. Peptides are a wild west, with vendors often labelling them as “for research use only” to dodge regulators.

In parallel, drugmakers are looking for scientifically proven ways to add healthy years—a far more arduous process. America’s Food and Drug Administration (FDA) does not treat ageing as a disease, so there is no route to approving a medicine that slows it. Would-be longevity drugs must instead win approval to treat a specific condition, often one linked to ageing, and then try to expand to others.

GLP-1s show how that might work. First approved for diabetes and then obesity, these drugs have since been shown to help with heart disease, sleep apnoea and kidney problems, all of which become more common with age. By lowering the risk of such conditions, the drugs may thus help people live longer. At a conference last month Lilly and Novo, its Danish rival, presented data suggesting that patients taking their GLP-1s were ageing more slowly. The yardstick was “ageing clocks”, which estimate how old a body really is (as opposed to how many birthdays it has had) from chemical marks on DNA or the mix of proteins in the blood. Novo found the biological age of the hearts of patients on its GLP-1s to be up to four years younger compared with those on a placebo, though all were overweight or diabetic. Lilly calls its own results preliminary.

Whatever GLP-1s turn out to do for ageing, they have already changed how big pharma thinks about the opportunity. Five or ten years ago drugmakers were chasing rare diseases, says Stephen Roper of L.E.K., a consultancy. But GLP-1s have re-established the appeal of mass-market drugs.

Rather than develop longevity treatments themselves, pharma giants mostly buy options on biotechs’ work. Lilly has struck a deal with Insilico worth up to $2.75bn. Novartis, a Swiss drugmaker, has one worth up to $550m with BioAge Labs, another biotech. The ranks of such startups are growing. Last year longevity biotechs raised $18.4bn, more than in the previous ten years combined (see chart).

Insilico calls its products “dual-purpose therapeutics”, each targeting ageing and a specific disease at the same time. A drug aimed only at ageing, argues Dr Zhavoronkov, its boss, would struggle to attract serious investors. Insilico’s most advanced candidate, rentosertib, treats idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, a disease that scars the lungs. It entered a late-stage trial in July, making it one of the furthest along of any drug designed with ageing in mind. In an earlier trial of 42 patients, ageing clocks suggested that those on the drug were biologically younger than those on a placebo, by around three years on some measures, though all were already ill.

Other startups are looking to reverse ageing altogether. They include Mr Altman’s Retro; Altos Labs; and NewLimit, co-founded by Brian Armstrong, a crypto entrepreneur, which in June announced $435m in fresh funding. Most are betting on “epigenetic reprogramming”, the idea that the chemical switches on DNA, which become muddled with age, can be reset.

Previous efforts by drugmakers to create longevity treatments have ended in disappointment. In 2008 Britain’s GSK bought Sirtris, a biotech developing drugs inspired by resveratrol, a compound in red wine. Five years later it shut the firm down. Calico, launched by Google in 2013 to tackle ageing, has achieved little. Unity Biotechnology, a startup focused on clearing out ageing cells, laid off its entire staff in May last year after disappointing trials.

The new wave of biotech founders and investors argue this time will be different, thanks in part to AI, which they hope will accelerate discoveries. The first human trials for a drug targeting epigenetic reprogramming—a liver treatment developed by NewLimit—may begin next year. While the results are gathered, consumers will keep seeking immortality elsewhere. ■

item.title: AI正让保护主义者变成自由贸易者
item.description:
Finance & economics

财经版块 | 全球化反击 2026年11月5日 一年半前，唐纳德·特朗普意气风发，一心逆转全球化。在 Americans 为生活成本忧心忡忡之际，这位自称“关税侠”的人物宣布“慢性贸易逆差”为“国家紧急状态”，并对进口商品加征高额关税。保护主义情绪蔓延开来。8月，印度总理纳伦德拉·莫迪呼吁同胞拥抱 swadeshi（自给自足），坚称“任何一件外国东西”都不应进入他们的家庭。欧盟将钢铁进口关税提高一倍。墨西哥对来自中国及其他亚洲经济体的商品征收高额关税。世界贸易组织（WTO）和国际货币基金组织（IMF）的经济学家编制的一项指数显示，仅2025年一年，限制性贸易措施就增加了60%以上。 然而，尽...
item.content:encoded:
AI正让保护主义者变成自由贸易者

财经版块 | 全球化反击 2026年11月5日

一年半前，唐纳德·特朗普意气风发，一心逆转全球化。在 Americans 为生活成本忧心忡忡之际，这位自称“关税侠”的人物宣布“慢性贸易逆差”为“国家紧急状态”，并对进口商品加征高额关税。保护主义情绪蔓延开来。8月，印度总理纳伦德拉·莫迪呼吁同胞拥抱 swadeshi（自给自足），坚称“任何一件外国东西”都不应进入他们的家庭。欧盟将钢铁进口关税提高一倍。墨西哥对来自中国及其他亚洲经济体的商品征收高额关税。世界贸易组织（WTO）和国际货币基金组织（IMF）的经济学家编制的一项指数显示，仅2025年一年，限制性贸易措施就增加了60%以上。

然而，尽管保护主义情绪高涨，如今的全球贸易却一派繁荣。自2024年第四季度（特朗普重返白宫前夕）以来，全球贸易的美元价值飙升了27%以上。今年增速还在加快。2026年前八个月，贸易额较去年同期增长18%，以历史标准衡量，这一速度相当惊人。即便按贸易量计算，预计贸易增速也将连续第二年超过世界经济增速——这是2007-09年金融危机前全球化鼎盛时期的标志。

自由贸易者可以感谢人工智能。随着企业竞相建设数据中心，为其提供动力的服务器、芯片和网络设备贸易量猛增。急于在国内建设AI能力的政府，基本上不对外国硬件征收关税。根据WTO对AI相关商品的分类，《经济学人》计算出，2026年前八个月此类产品的贸易额较去年同期激增55%。剔除AI相关商品后，世界贸易仍在增长，但增速远没那么亮眼（见图表1上图）。AI硬件约占世界进口的四分之一，而2023年这一比例为15%。看来，保护主义者在符合自身利益时，也学会了爱上自由贸易。

美国的AI贸易最为活跃。目前，在计算机、电信设备和数据中心建设上的支出占GDP的2.5%。几乎所有设备都来自国外：据美联储数据，美国每在高科技设备上投资1美元，就会进口约90美分的设备。AI相关商品的进口额今年有望突破惊人的1万亿美元。因此，全球最大进口国并未完全按计划退出全球化。自2024年底以来，美国的商品进口增长了16%，大致与2018年至2024年的趋势持平。但AI热潮改变了美国从国外购买的商品结构。我们计算得出，2026年前八个月，AI相关产品的进口额较去年同期飙升69%。其他所有商品的进口额则下降了10%（见图表1下图）。三年前，美国进口的汽车、石油、药品和金属是服务器、芯片和网络设备的五倍多。如今，后者已略占上风。

自2025年4月“解放日”关税以来，特朗普大体上对推动AI热潮的硬件网开一面。明尼阿波利斯联储一位经济学家的研究显示，高达97%的计算机硬件进口和85%的网络设备进口属于关税豁免类别。2025年，山姆大叔征收的关税相当于进口计算机和网络设备价值的不到2%，而对与AI无关的商品征收的关税则接近10%。即便是今年1月出台的冠冕堂皇的“半导体关税”也漏洞百出。这项25%的关税主要针对英伟达H200等先进芯片，这些芯片从台湾运往中国途中必须经过美国检查。对美国数据中心、初创企业、研究机构及其他国内用途的豁免范围之广，以至于无党派的国会研究服务处（Congressional Research Service）都质疑，受影响的芯片进口是否真的会有任何一笔缴纳关税。

这位保护主义旗手对自由贸易的拥抱，却让他缩减美国贸易逆差的雄心变得复杂起来。9月，商品贸易逆差达到1360亿美元，较去年同期扩大逾70%，进口总额创下历史新高。对国外AI硬件的需求是部分原因。美国占全球服务器、计算机零部件和网络设备进口的四成，而其他商品仅占六分之一。其此类设备的出口规模远不足以抵消这些采购。结果是，美国在主要经济体中拥有迄今最大的AI相关贸易逆差（见图表2上图）。如果近年来AI相关商品的进口增速与其他进口相同，那么2025年的商品贸易逆差将缩小16%，即近2000亿美元。

这一切都表明，用贸易逆差来判断经济成败是多么愚蠢。一台在海外组装的服务器进入美国时，会恶化商品贸易平衡。但安装在美国数据中心后，它就变成了生产性资本，在未来多年持续产生算力。美联储的研究发现，以往由技术驱动的投资热潮扩大了经常账户逆差，但同时提高了产出。自由贸易让美国企业能够专注于自己最擅长的事——从芯片设计到AI研究和软件——同时依赖海外专业制造商提供设备。

与此同时，AI迷宫般的供应链揭示了“回流”的局限。六个经济体——台湾、墨西哥、越南、泰国、韩国和马来西亚——占美国AI进口的五分之四以上（见图表2下图）。仅墨西哥和台湾就供应了美国AI服务器及其他计算机处理设备进口的85%。尽管其中会包含一些转道货物，但中国在此类进口中的可见份额已大幅下降，六经济体之外的其他国家也是如此。

以一台运往美国数据中心的英伟达GB300 AI服务器机架为例。其芯片在美国设计，在台湾利用配备德国制造精密反射镜的荷兰光刻机制造，并搭配韩国擅长的高带宽内存。随后，包含72颗强大AI芯片的18个计算托盘从台湾运往墨西哥，由当地工人将冷却系统、电源模块、网络交换机以及来自中国和越南的零部件组装在一起。组装完成的机架随后北上越过边境。这还只是简化版本。即便是现正由台湾最大芯片制造商在亚利桑那州制造的英伟达Blackwell AI芯片，也必须运回亚洲，与高带宽内存进行封装。

特朗普对自由贸易那不太可能的拥抱也有其限度，即便在AI领域也是如此。他对钢铁、铝和铜征收的关税正在推高数据中心的建设成本，从建筑材料到冷却系统的一切都变得更贵。智库战略与国际研究中心（CSIS）估计，现有的金属关税到2030年可能为美国计划中的数据中心建设增加1300亿美元成本。更糟的还在后头。总统正在考虑对半导体及含半导体的产品征收更广泛的关税，可能包括为美国AI热潮提供动力的服务器。CSIS估计，全面征收25%的关税可能使数据中心建设成本增加3600亿美元。

或许11月3日的中期选举会让政府三思。美国人曾喜欢关税的想法，直到由此导致价格上涨。如今，他们正在重新发现自己内心的自由贸易者。根据选举之夜的民调，约三分之二的选民认为特朗普的关税损害了经济。对生活成本的不满帮助民主党大获全胜。不过，即便总统不领这个情，经验证明全球化也是一件难以扼杀的东西。■

item.content:encoded:
密集型育儿不再是富人的专利

财经版块 | 全世界的虎妈们，联合起来 2026年11月5日 富有的父母与众不同。他们有钱。他们过去也曾不同，因为会把大把的钱花在子女的教育上。然而，随着大学入学名额和高薪工作的竞争日益激烈，各个收入水平的父母都在更早、更积极地投资子女的未来。从幼儿的钢琴课到青少年的网球课，密集型育儿正在兴起。相关花费数额可观。超过一半的美国儿童在放学后或周末参加一项体育运动。2024年，仅一个孩子的一项主要运动，平均每个家庭就要花费1016美元。这比2019年上涨了46%，是同期通胀率的两倍。除了每周多次接送孩子参加训练以及与教练沟通等后勤事务外，美国父母每周还要投入超过15小时在孩子的体育运动上——这相当于一份兼职工作的时间投入。年轻的身体如此，年轻的心灵亦然。在亚洲较富裕的地区，私人补习长期以来一直备受追捧。根据全国性调查，2025年，四分之三的韩国学龄儿童参加了付费补习班，其中收入最低的五分之一群体中也有57%的人参加。五岁儿童中也有五分之四在上补习班。经合组织（OECD）——一个主要由富裕国家组成的俱乐部——估计，每个学生平均补习支出已达到家庭平均可支配收入的十分之一左右。 如今，其他亚洲父母也开始大把花钱。印度约27%的学生（城市地区为31%）接受私人辅导。在中国，教育支出增长最快的是最贫困地区。这一趋势并不局限于亚洲。法国15至18岁的学生中有三分之一报名参加了私人辅导。在英国，就读公立学校的学生中，最贫困家庭和最富裕家庭获得补习机会的比例如今几乎持平；根据教育慈善机构萨顿信托（Sutton Trust）的数据，收入最低四分之一家庭的学生中有37%获得补习，略低于收入最高四分之一家庭的39%。在伦敦，公立学校学生的这一比例升至45%（见图表1）。这一差距的缩小在一定程度上得益于政府资助补习计划的扩大。但家长也在自掏腰包：萨顿信托的数据显示，在公立学校就读的11至16岁英国青少年中，30%表示接受过私人补习，高于2005年的18%。伦敦经济学院的Matthias Doepke和耶鲁大学的Fabrizio Zilibotti发现，从历史上看，一个国家的不平等程度越高，父母对独立性或想象力等软性品质的关注就越少（见图表2）。西方民众认为不平等现象正在加剧，中产阶级生活方式被视为不再理所当然，这意味着父母们变得不那么放松了。他们的关注点正转向勤奋等品质，而这正是密集型育儿试图灌输的。 高压教育也带来了日益高昂的成本。根据国际研究项目“国民转移账户”（National Transfer Accounts）的数据，1990年，美国在中小学和大学以及补习、辅导等方面的私人支出，占终身教育总投资（包括公共支出）的18%。到2020年（可获得的最新数据），这一比例达到24%，相当于6.8万美元。2023年，韩国每个孩子的人均私人支出占终身教育投资的42%，达到令人瞠目的15.2万美元（同样以2020年美元计算）。然而，这些投资并不一定能转化为社会流动性。这可能是因为，尽管穷人支出更多，但富人并未放松。在过去十年中，法国和西班牙的子女比父母过得更好的可能性停滞不前，而在新加坡和韩国则大幅下降。进入顶尖大学比以往任何时候都难。哈佛大学的录取率为3%，而1960年为30%。北京大学录取的农村学生比例从1978年至1998年间的三分之一，下降到2021年的六分之一左右——这一降幅快于中国农村人口的相对减少速度。萨顿信托的数据显示，即使拥有学位，出身于非大学生家庭的美国人中有30%能达到收入最高的五分之一群体，而父母上过大学的人中这一比例为41%。尽管在过去十年中，出身非大学生家庭的成年人获得大学学位的比例上升了10个百分点，但这类人群预期能获得的大学教育收入溢价却下降了11个百分点。智库决议基金会（Resolution Foundation）的数据显示，在英国，在贫困中长大（以是否有资格享受免费校餐来界定）的大学毕业生，在从同一所大学同一专业毕业十年后，收入比同龄人低7%。在子女未来的竞争中，富有的父母仍占优势。■

item.content:encoded:
美国租客深陷困境

财经版块 | 逾期 2026年11月5日

31岁的雅各布·拉米雷斯是一家咖啡连锁店的运营经理，长期以来入不敷出。大学时他用信用卡买教科书；毕业后，他偶尔用信用卡付房租和水电费。到2022年，他和妻子以及他们的狗住在洛杉矶东部波莫纳的一间一居室公寓里。但不断上涨的房租和其他开销——“就像一条蟒蛇把我越勒越紧”——让他负债更深。2023年，拉米雷斯在五张卡上欠下2.8万美元，他求助了一家非营利性债务咨询机构。他有望在2028年前还清债务。

得益于人工智能热潮和强劲的消费支出，美国经济正在稳步增长。但三四年来，房主和像拉米雷斯这样的租客之间出现了一道鸿沟——租客占美国家庭的三分之一。《经济学人》的一项分析表明，租客越来越频繁地拖欠付款，并转向昂贵的高息短期信贷，而房主的财务状况依然稳健。美国正在经历一场“租客衰退”吗？他们的困境代表着一个转折。在2007年至2009年的全球金融危机期间，遭受痛苦的是房主。到2010年，每20笔抵押贷款中就有1笔丧失赎回权，十分之一违约。房价下跌了近四分之一；近四分之一的房主欠款超过了房产价值。

如今轮到租客承受更多痛苦。美联储上月发布的最新《消费者财务状况调查》（SCF）显示，在过去一年中，超过八分之一的消费者至少有一笔贷款还款逾期60天，这是自1989年有记录以来的最高比例（见图表1）。美联储在2025年末的另一项调查发现，四分之一的人在上个月没有全额付清所有账单，而抵押贷款持有人中这一比例为十分之一（见图表2）。约有六分之一的人觉得“难以维持生计”，是抵押贷款持有人比例的三倍多。

这种差距部分反映了人口结构。租客往往更年轻、更穷、受教育程度更低：2025年他们的家庭收入中位数为5.7万美元，而房主为10.3万美元。但我们计算得出，这些特征解释了租客与抵押贷款持有人之间差距的五分之三。剩下的呢？部分原因在于房租。根据政府机构人口普查局的数据，自2019年以来，美国房租上涨了42%，而租客的家庭收入仅增长34%。抵押贷款持有人的住房成本超出收入的比例也大致相当。但这在很大程度上反映了新购房者的月供更高——贷款机构已经审核过他们的还款能力，而且他们的抵押贷款利率通常固定数年。租客则在租约到期时面临更高的租金，无论他们是否负担得起。

其次，缺乏可依靠的储蓄。根据消费者财务状况调查，典型租客的流动储蓄为2000美元，而抵押贷款持有人为1.2万美元。房主通常还拥有更大的投资组合。“许多房主通过从经纪账户中取款来维持支出。”摩根大通研究所（一家银行内部智库）的特德·盖尔表示。疫情后学生贷款还款的恢复加剧了压力，这约占近期租客债务拖欠增加量的一半，但在抵押贷款持有人中仅占约四分之一。租客正在推迟支付其他账单。根据我们使用FINRA基金会数据进行的计算，在控制收入、年龄和其他人口因素后，租客从原本比抵押贷款持有人更不可能产生信用卡滞纳金，变成更可能产生滞纳金。一些租客转向其他形式的短期借贷。美联储的另一项调查发现，2025年有超过十分之一的租客申请了发薪日贷款或工资预支，几乎是2019年的两倍。储蓄只能搁置：“随着房租上涨，储蓄的能力——无论是为首付、应急还是其他——确实变得困难得多。”哈佛大学住房研究联合中心的惠特尼·艾尔古德-奥布里茨基表示。还有一些像拉米雷斯这样的人正在寻求帮助。一旦债务还清，他希望开始为自己买房存钱。其他人的路则要漫长得多。■

item.title: 市场如何看待中期选举
item.description:
Finance & economics

item.content:encoded:
市场如何看待中期选举

财经版块 | 波澜与涟漪 2026年11月5日 在地质学中，地震引发海啸。在美国政治中，蓝色海啸正在引发地震。在11月3日的中期选举中，民主党势如破竹。深红色的得克萨斯州数十年来首次选出蓝色参议员，深红堪萨斯州更是近一个世纪以来的首次。截至本文发稿时，唐纳德·特朗普上次以23个百分点优势赢下的密西西比州参议员选举，胜负仍难以预料。在金融市场上，对这些地震性事件的反应在很大程度上不过是耸耸肩。涵盖美国大公司的标普500指数在次日早间小幅上扬，收盘时上涨1.6%。十年期国债收益率小幅下行。美元轻微走弱。投资者的漠不关心可以理解。他们喜欢确定性，而民主党浪潮排除了无休止争议选举甚至宪法危机的噩梦情景。选举之夜，在共和党溃败的规模明朗之后，特朗普先生告诉《纽约时报》，他将接受结果。姑且称之为“呼——”效应。市场还喜欢两党分治政府带来的必然僵局——至少在美国是这样，那里的商业环境已经十分有利（政治瘫痪在欧洲等根本条件不利于增长的地方更成问题）。如果说有什么影响的话，一个重获活力的国会的监督可能会让总统更难提高关税、发动战争和削弱公共部门。围绕预算的争斗不可避免，但无论如何它们本来也会发生。而且民主党人往往不像共和党人那样愿意通过阻挠提高联邦债务上限来冒主权违约的风险。 尽管如此，表面的平静掩盖了底下的更多翻腾，尤其是在股票市场（见图表）。输家之一是埃隆·马斯克。这位一度身家万亿的右翼富豪浪费了近5亿美元，试图在今年选举中帮助共和党人胜出。民主党人将以仔细审查政府与他的汽车制造商特斯拉及其火箭公司SpaceX的合同作为回敬。这两家公司股价分别下跌了3%和4%。其他联邦承包商在民主党人中不会激起那么多个人敌意。但现在反对党掌控了钱袋子，他们仍然可以预期受到审视，尤其是在左派反感行业中。私营监狱运营商如CoreCivic和GEO都曾协助特朗普先生冷酷的大规模驱逐行动，由于担心新一届国会将压缩移民预算，它们的股价下跌。民主党人也不太可能接受特朗普先生提出的1.5万亿美元国防开支请求，这将打击洛克希德·马丁、诺斯罗普·格鲁曼、RTX和其他军工企业。第二组输家是命运完全依赖人工智能数据中心建设的公司。这些设施曾得到许多共和党人的支持——直到它们引发反弹，而民主党人无情地利用了这一点。在占计划新增产能一半的四个州中，佐治亚、俄亥俄和得克萨斯三个州的州长是共和党人。从明年起，这四个州都将有民主党州长。数据中心首选目的地得克萨斯州，当选州长吉娜·伊诺霍萨在竞选中承诺立即暂停数据中心建设。大型独立数据中心运营商CoreWeave的股价随即大跌10%。生产AI服务器存储芯片的美光科技市值蒸发了7%。AI芯片制造巨头、市值5万亿美元的英伟达下滑3%。电气元件制造商——数据中心及为其供电的发电厂需要大量此类元件——也受到了冲击。选举前，两党曾就一项法案达成初步协议，该法案将使管道和风电场等大型能源项目更容易获得必要许可。民主党人现在可能希望争取更有利的条件。GE Vernova、Vistra和Vertiv的股价各自下跌了约十分之一。相反，蓝色浪潮提振了那些可以指望特朗普式预算削减被逆转的行业（医疗保健和清洁能源）以及数据中心的大金主。大型科技公司的“超大规模云厂商”现在可能减少支出，保住利润率，同时在现有产能上面对来自CoreWeave等公司的竞争也会减少。亚马逊和微软上涨超过6%。Alphabet上涨逾3%。就连由大男子主义的马克·扎克伯格领导的Meta也小幅上扬。科技老板们可以预期被召到国会参加充满敌意的听证会，既涉及人工智能，也涉及他们对特朗普先生的谄媚态度。但至少他们的下一次财报电话会议可能会更加友好。■

item.title: Indebted tycoons haunt China’s banking system
item.description:

item.content:encoded:
Indebted tycoons haunt China’s banking system

Finance & economics | Collateral damage

Nov 5th 2026

ON OCTOBER 31ST Bank of Shanghai gave investors a nasty shock. It said its net profit had collapsed by 93% in the third quarter, year on year, to 350m yuan ($53m); its non-performing loans shot up by 75% in the first nine months of 2026; and the capital set aside to cover unexpected losses hit the lowest in a decade. Its share price plunged by over 10%. The main source of the lender’s troubles seems to be its relationship with one man, Yao Zhenhua.

Mr Yao has been stalking Chinese finance since 2015. That year his conglomerate, Baoneng, made a hostile bid for Vanke, a giant property developer. This was a triple surprise: such takeovers are almost unheard of in China; they are entirely unheard of when the target is, like Vanke, partly state-owned; and Baoneng financed the deal in an unconventional way, using premiums from several insurers it owned. This brazenness earned Mr Yao the nickname “barbarian”, in tribute to American corporate raiders of the late 1980s.

The takeover failed and Mr Yao’s use of premiums was found to be illegal (China tightly regulates how they can be invested). In 2017 he was banned from the insurance industry for ten years. But he expanded his empire in other areas. This included a 6.6bn yuan debt-fuelled investment in Qoros, a maker of electric cars. As Bank of Shanghai has disclosed, commercial conquest has not gone well for the barbarian.

As part of a long-running lawsuit against Mr Yao and Baoneng, the lender has sought to recover loans extended to his companies worth at least 12.9bn yuan. The loans were secured in 2020 with property and with personal guarantees from Mr Yao. This collateral took a hit when China’s property sector imploded. Qoros, meanwhile, sold too few cars and folded. In January this year Mr Yao, whose poor credit score bans him from commercial flights and luxury hotels, appeared in a social-media post claiming that local government officials had cheated him out of his investment in the car firm.

The most stunning revelation from Bank of Shanghai is that Mr Yao and his companies have “no executable assets” from which to recover those debts. This would explain photos posted to social media of someone looking remarkably like him riding the metro in Shenzhen, a big southern city, rather than taking a limo. More importantly for Bank of Shanghai’s investors, it explains what happened to the lender’s profits, which were eaten up by huge impairment losses. Many other Chinese banks that have done business with Mr Yao and Baoneng may be next.

Mr Yao is not the first tycoon to rattle the banking system. In 2019 another, Xiao Jianhua, caused a mini financial crisis. He is in prison. A fellow indebted plutocrat, Lai Xiaomin, was executed in 2021. Despite the Communist Party’s efforts to rid Chinese finance of such rogues, the Baoneng barbarian is probably not the last.■

item.content:encoded:
中国股市的困境是一个警示

财经版块 | Buttonwood 2026年11月5日 在美好的旧时光里，中国以全球最伟大的趋同故事吸引投资者。它的生活水平将赶上西方，经济规模将成倍增长，股市价值也将随之上升。或者故事就是这样讲的。投资者只需要在其他所有人之前站在历史的正确一边。近年来，中国对全球投资者的剩余吸引力建立在相反的逻辑上——不是趋同，而是多元化。关于中国命运的谈论少了，对其特殊性的认知多了。已经很清楚的是，中国随着共产党自己的鼓点起舞。这意味着它可以逆全球趋势而行，无论是好是坏。最近的一个例子是股市。根据MSCI世界指数，尽管近期有所波动，今年全球股市仍上涨了11%。韩国和台湾等其他东亚经济体借助人工智能繁荣涨得更高。中国也紧密嵌入人工智能供应链，并拥有多家创新的模型制造商，包括在香港上市的Z.ai和MiniMax等公司。但今年下半年，中国科技股在境内外均大幅下跌。其蓝筹股指数沪深300在2026年迄今下跌超过11%。中国股票将同步性变成了特殊性。

中国政府似乎对这种特殊性的来源感到厌倦。暴跌促使“国家队”——即在需要时支撑市场的国有金融机构——重新买入。中国央行也伸出了援手。11月2日，它表示将重新启用一项帮助保险公司和券商等机构投资者获得购买股票所需流动性抵押品的计划。它还将降低公司借贷回购自家股票的成本。

为什么股市萎靡不振？部分原因与中国特色有关。以财政政策为例。其他大型经济体本会受益于预算约束，但几乎看不到这种约束。相比之下，中国政府在本应放松的时候却在勒紧腰带。高盛估计，按广义口径计算，今年中国的财政赤字将收窄GDP的1.4%。无休止的房地产低迷也仍在造成损害。10月29日，信用评级机构惠誉表示，可能下调珠海华发集团发行的债券评级。该集团是一家位于中国珠三角的国有企业集团，以其俯瞰珠海和澳门沿海城市的72层高楼而闻名，同时背负着4130亿元人民币（合620亿美元）的巨额债务。据彭博社报道，该集团最近推迟了两只信托产品（不在交易所交易的债务工具）的付款，并要求延长银行贷款期限。其上市地产子公司的股价下跌超过五分之一——尽管该集团的主要所有者珠海市不太可能让其违约公开交易的债券。

对中国表现不佳的另一个解释更令人担忧。它可能是一种似乎正在世界范围内蔓延的投资趋势的早期受害者：对人工智能热情的消退。在西方，投资者开始担心人工智能模型最终将商品化。随着创新者难以维持对模仿者的持久领先，定价权将消失。在中国，那种严峻的终局或多或少是这个行业的起点。中国的人工智能实验室公开分享了让模型变得聪明的数学“权重”。这促进了采用，并帮助实验室吸引了既受知识荣耀又受财务成功激励的精英人才。但开放性是有商业代价的。根据研究公司Epoch AI的数据，中国六家领先公司的人工智能相关收入合计约为美国前两大公司OpenAI和Anthropic总收入之和的十分之一。

中国也可能预示了当新科技股供应最终赶上需求时会发生什么。它用拥挤的首次公开募股渠道考验了投资者的胃口。美国可能会发现，Anthropic备受期待的上市即使在其大得多的市场中也会引发类似的消化不良。中国的奇特之处让许多全球投资者望而却步。科技界更大的担忧是，中国今日的瘦身成为世界其他地区未来的写照。中国可能与其说是一个异类，不如说是一个预兆。■

item.content:encoded:
威廉·诺德豪斯，左右翼都钟爱的经济学家

财经 | 自由交流 2026年11月5日

威廉·诺德豪斯对自己专业工具的信心坚定不移。数十年间，他一直在耶鲁大学经济学系效力——他于1967年来到这里，年仅26岁，一直工作到10月30日去世。他编辑了《经济学》教科书，至今仍被美国本科生使用。他坚信经济学方法可以惠及其他学科，将书斋里的课题搁置一旁，投身于让政策制定者殚精竭虑的辩论：气候、技术和税收。这份信念使他毫不退缩，也无惧争斗。在他那一代经济学家中，没有谁涉猎过如此广泛且充满争议的议题。他开创了碳定价（这帮助他赢得了2018年诺贝尔奖），取悦了美国的进步派，也惹恼了保守派。他还为亿万富翁辩护，效果则截然相反。因此，他成为了一位罕见的、同时赢得左翼和右翼尊重的经济学家。

经济学依赖价格体系。诺德豪斯毕生致力于计算那些缺失的价格。他的博士论文考察了知识经济中的此类失灵，并提出了最优专利期限，以减少对可复制创意的投资不足，同时最大化社会福利。上世纪70年代，他认定构建技术变革的理论模型“太难”（于是将这个任务留给了与他共享诺贝尔奖的保罗·罗默）。于是，他转而研究气候变化。尽管气候经济学的实践日后变得充满政治争议，但其理论尚属可控。经济增长依赖能源。生产和消耗能源的企业并没有承担由此产生的碳污染成本。随之而来的变暖可能损害增长。该怎么办？麻省理工学院的一个研究小组倾向于彻底放弃增长。诺德豪斯不同意。他认为，问题在于缺乏一个将科学方程与经济方程结合起来、把增长、排放和环境联系在一起的模型。

诺德豪斯花了接下来二十年试图构建这样一个模型。1992年，他发表了一篇论文，勾勒出“动态综合气候经济”（DICE）模型的轮廓。其20多个方程最终涵盖了他教给本科生的基础经济学方程，到关于灾难风险的科学预测，再到人类如何适应更炎热世界的预测。再加上一个贴现率——即相对于当下，对未来世代生命的价值评估——该模型就能得出减排路径：既不会因能源生产不足而使今天数百万人陷入贫困，也不会因全球变暖摧毁经济而让明天数百万人陷入困境。让世界走上这条路径的碳价格，等于减少一吨额外二氧化碳排放的成本与这吨二氧化碳未来造成损害的成本相等时的价格。

随着对气候变化的担忧日益加剧，人们对这项研究的兴趣也与日俱增。到2010年，巴拉克·奥巴马政府已将DICE模型纳入美国政策。诺德豪斯的气候经济学也有批评者。他与尼古拉斯·斯特恩进行了长期论战，后者更重视未来世代的权重。一些气候科学家认为他低估了灾难性事件的概率，并质疑他DICE论文的结论——即经济上最优的结果是允许全球平均气温比工业化前水平上升3°C。然而，即使他们挑战他的一些数值假设，他的批评者也乐于在他的框架内开展工作。

DICE让诺德豪斯成为气候名人。但这不过是他庞大冰山般学术产出的冰山一角。他1975年的一篇论文提出，政客们会在选举前几个月放松货币政策以降低失业率来拉票——这一观点催生了大量类似的政治经济学研究。1996年，他比较了不同时代用现代灯泡产生相当于一小时光照的成本。他的结论是，这一成本从1800年工人劳动5.4小时骤降到1992年的不到半秒，这意味着传统价格指数大大低估了生活水平的提升。

他最终又回到了博士时代关注的问题。2005年，他利用美国1948年至2001年的数据计算出，发明者只获得了其发明为社会带来价值的4%。换言之，创新者的经济贡献远超其个人财富。这篇论文发表之时，美国正涌现出新一代科技亿万富翁，其论点受到这些富豪捍卫者的推崇。如果白手起家的大亨们为社会贡献了如此之多，为什么还要对他们征更多的税？就连进步派加州人似乎也认同：在11月3日的中期选举中，该州大多数选民似乎否决了一项对亿万富翁财富征税的投票提案。

最重要的是，诺德豪斯的经济学是实用主义的胜利。他相信将杂乱无章的问题塑造成可理解的框架，并接受其带来的所有含义，无论把你引向何方。他认为，产出有用的数字有时比精确更为重要。他在1987年的一篇论文中提出，最好的经济预测是融合了最多信息的预测（他早在十年前做出的知情预测——全球气温到如今大约会上升1°C——准确无误）。他也将开放心态传授给耶鲁的学生们，讲座结束后总是耐心回答他们的提问——由于提问人数众多，常常一答就是几个小时。另一次开明慷慨的展示是，他将自己调查光照成本时获得的一盏古代巴比伦油灯赠予了诺贝尔博物馆。与他奉献给经济学的思想遗产相比，这不过是微微一闪。■

item.title: 天文学家被天空中的小红点弄得困惑不解
item.description:
Science & technology

科学与技术 | 连线 2026年11月5日 当詹姆斯·韦伯太空望远镜（JWST）——一台围绕太阳运行的高分辨率相机——于2022年开始向地球传回图像时，天文学家们看到了一些奇怪的东西。除了他们预期会看到的各式各样的宇宙角色——恒星、星系、星云等等——还有一小撮微小的红色光点，或者用专业术语来说，“小红点”。天文学家们完全不知道它们是什么。在寻找答案的过程中，他们将目光投向了宇宙中最神秘的物体——黑洞。对一些天文学家来说，这些红点是正处于空前剧烈增长期的黑洞。对另一些人来说，它们是奇特的、类似恒星的物体，中心有黑洞。弄清楚这一点很重要：这些红点可能揭示出位于星系中心的超大质量黑洞的起源，并解释...
item.content:encoded:
天文学家被天空中的小红点弄得困惑不解

科学与技术 | 连线 2026年11月5日 当詹姆斯·韦伯太空望远镜（JWST）——一台围绕太阳运行的高分辨率相机——于2022年开始向地球传回图像时，天文学家们看到了一些奇怪的东西。除了他们预期会看到的各式各样的宇宙角色——恒星、星系、星云等等——还有一小撮微小的红色光点，或者用专业术语来说，“小红点”。天文学家们完全不知道它们是什么。在寻找答案的过程中，他们将目光投向了宇宙中最神秘的物体——黑洞。对一些天文学家来说，这些红点是正处于空前剧烈增长期的黑洞。对另一些人来说，它们是奇特的、类似恒星的物体，中心有黑洞。弄清楚这一点很重要：这些红点可能揭示出位于星系中心的超大质量黑洞的起源，并解释它们为何能如此迅速地变得如此巨大。缅因州科尔比学院的天文学家戴尔·科切夫斯基说，这场辩论十分激烈。“我从未见过这样的情况。”已知的情况是，这些小红点不出意料地很小——宽度通常不到银河系的0.5%——而且呈红色，发出的亮光富含较长、较红的波长。它们也很古老。宇宙中第一批小红点诞生于134亿年前的宇宙黎明时期，当时宇宙的年龄约为5亿年——距离第一批星系出现后不久。自从这些红点首次被发现以来，已有500多个被报告，而且数量还在继续增加。夏威夷大学的天文学家罗汉·奈杜说：“你拍的每一张图像里，都会看到其中一个物体正注视着你。”他是首创这个术语的团队的一员。“所以它们一定很重要。”当天文学家第一次看到这些小红点时，他们认为这些物体是数量众多的成熟星系的辉光。但如此成熟的星系在宇宙大爆炸后这么快的时间内不可能有足够的时间形成。这导致一些人将这些红点称为“宇宙破坏者”，它们的存在暗示宇宙可能比人们以前认为的更古老。然后，在2023年初，科切夫斯基博士和他的同事们在红点产生的光谱中发现了一种独特的模式。它表明这些红点被一团致密、快速运动的氢气体所包围。要让气体以所需的速度运动，需要巨大的引力。这不利于“宇宙破坏者”星系假说，因为它们恒星之间的距离很大，会使引力相对较小。相反，大量的质量需要被集中在极小的体积内。这正是对黑洞的完美描述。但这似乎是矛盾的。黑洞的引力如此之强，以至于连光都无法逃脱它们的掌控：那么，它们怎么可能发光呢？答案是，当物质落入黑洞时（这一过程被称为吸积），物质在升温时会发出辐射。如果一个黑洞足够大，这种辐射可以极其强烈。例如，活动星系核（AGN）——大多数星系中心的吸积超大质量黑洞——是宇宙中最明亮的光源之一。因此，吸积黑洞可能是JWST所看到的小红点亮度的来源。而且，虽然普通的活动星系核被环形的气体和尘埃包围，但构成尘埃的重元素在宇宙历史的早期可能没有时间形成。科切夫斯基博士说：“可能气体太多，以至于那个环形变成了茧状。”“它完全包裹住了那个东西。”光与氢气相互作用后也会变红。但有一个问题。活动星系核在物质落入时升温也会释放X射线。然而，小红点几乎不发射任何X射线。为了解释这一点，活动星系核假说的支持者提出，中心黑洞正在以异常高的速率吸积。正如一列火车上人群争相上车时很难下车一样，落入物质的堆积限制了有多少X射线能够穿透。对科切夫斯基博士来说，这种解释的吸引力归结为奥卡姆剃刀原则：“这些是我们已知的事物，只是稍有改动。”然而，奈杜博士属于更具想象力的阵营。“我们只需要承认这是一种全新的天体物理物体，”他说。奈杜博士和他的同事们提出，小红点既不是恒星也不是黑洞，而是兼具两者特征的东西。然而，他们的想象力并没有延伸到命名上：他们把这些新奇物体称为“黑洞恒星”。 像活动星系核一样，黑洞恒星是一个被气体茧包裹的吸积黑洞。但这个茧的密度要大得多。事实上，密度如此之大，以至于黑洞吸积物质发出的任何辐射——无论是光还是X射线——都无法直接逃逸。相反，辐射被最内层的气体吸收，使其发出新的、波长更长的辐射，然后被下一层吸收。经过许多这样的阶段后，该假说的支持者说，光会从类似于恒星发光表面的外层逸出，带有独特的红色调。因此，这样的物体从外面看起来像恒星，但提供能量的不是核聚变，而是不断增长的黑洞。尽管这两种提议都在一定程度上解释了红点的独特特征，但两者都不能令人满意。活动星系核假说的批评者认为，它需要一系列假设来解释它们不寻常的外观。但黑洞恒星假说的支持者必须解释为什么少数红点显示出光从气体茧中泄漏出来，而它们的模型不允许这种情况发生。这场辩论中哪一方听起来更有说服力，可能归结为个人品味。正如普林斯顿大学的天文学家珍妮·格林所说：“人们看到他们想看到的东西。”什么能解决这个问题？答案可能在于红点的质量。这两种提议从相同的数据中预测出了截然不同的数字：类似活动星系核的物体可能比黑洞恒星重几个数量级。5月，由当时在剑桥大学的伊格纳斯·尤奥兹巴利斯领导的一个团队在《自然》杂志上发表了第一个小红点的质量测量结果。他们计算了气体茧不同部分运动的速度，并用它们来推断红点的质量。结果约为5000万个太阳质量，这是活动星系核假说阵营得分。但这项工作被证明是有争议的。尤奥兹巴利斯博士本人指出，这只是一个数据点。此外，“我认为他们做不到他们声称做了的事，”格林博士说。她认为，作者的技术只适用于测量明确定义物体的速度，比如两颗恒星，而不适用于小红点周围混乱气体茧内的运动。这不仅仅是学术上的认可以问题。例如，天文学家不知道第一批超大质量黑洞是如何增重的，也不知道这如何塑造了它们所在的星系。黑洞恒星适中的质量将表明它们从很小开始，通过吞食其气体茧而迅速增长。但如果活动星系核假说的支持者是对的，那么不知何故，第一批黑洞在诞生时就已经很巨大了。在这些问题上，小红点的分量远远超过它们看上去的分量。■

item.title: AI模型可以互相调整彼此的大脑
item.description:

item.content:encoded:
AI模型可以互相调整彼此的大脑

科学与技术 | 权重与尺度 2026年11月5日

像-0.180、-0.080和0.191这样的数字，对未经训练的普通人来说并没有太大意义。即使专家被告知这些是AI模型的“权重”——即其内部参数的称呼——他们也难以重建出这是哪种模型，或者它被训练用来做什么。但似乎一个前沿的大语言模型（LLM），比如OpenAI的GPT-6 Astra，就不会有这样的困难。这是麻省理工学院博士生Rikiya Takehi及其合作者在11月2日发布的一篇博客文章中提出的观点。他们声称，Astra仅通过查看另一个AI模型的权重，就推断出该模型是被训练来玩Pong——一款基础视频游戏——的。更令人印象深刻的是，它通过调整一个小型LLM的权重修复了一个已知错误，从而将其在一个流行数学测试中的分数提高了五倍，并且它还手动编程了一个能玩围棋（一种棋盘游戏）的AI模型的权重。如果普通的模型设计类似于自然选择，即通过设置外部条件让正确的权重自行涌现，那么Astra所做的调整则更接近基因工程。

这些说法迅速引起了该领域其他研究者的关注。一些观察者推测，未来的AI可能会调整自己的权重，从而可能释放出递归自我改进的失控列车。另一些人则希望AI系统能帮助他们深入观察未来的模型，尽早发现可能的不当行为。这篇博客文章并不能保证这些事情一定会实现。它展示的仅仅是模型在其他模型中发现问题并修复缺陷的相对简单示例，而这些模型本身仍然比Astra小数千倍。此外，牛津大学的AI研究员Fazl Barez（并未参与这项工作）表示，这种能力之所以出现，很可能只是因为该模型在之前的以人类为主导的实验中接受过做同样事情的训练。对前沿模型的全面理解仍然有很长的路要走。但如果这真的发生了，Barez博士说，“那将是我一生中最快乐的一天。”■

item.title: Drones don’t just blow up the enemy
item.description:
Science & technology

Science & technology | Ears in the sky Nov 5th 2026 In the David and Goliath war between Ukraine and Russia, drones have proved a great equaliser. Ukraine’s short-range aircraft are cutting Russia’s supply lines to its occupying troops, while long-range versions attack oil refineries, airfie...
item.content:encoded:
Drones don’t just blow up the enemy

Science & technology | Ears in the sky

Nov 5th 2026

In the David and Goliath war between Ukraine and Russia, drones have proved a great equaliser. Ukraine’s short-range aircraft are cutting Russia’s supply lines to its occupying troops, while long-range versions attack oil refineries, airfields and warehouses as far afield as Siberia.

Not all military drones, however, carry warheads. Many are used instead for spying and target location. A lot of these gather their data at optical or infrared frequencies. But some, involved in the field of signals intelligence, or SIGINT, listen out for radio waves. And within that category are those which seek not to understand what is being broadcast, but merely to identify and locate its source, the better to attack it—a field of endeavour called electronic support measures (ESM).

According to Thomas Withington, an electronic-warfare expert at the Royal United Services Institute, a think-tank, the result has been an arms race in which the radio frequencies used to control drones have migrated ever further up and down the spectrum, in attempts to evade detection. Frequency-hopping radios, which skip from one wavelength to another thousands of times a second, are getting faster, so a transmitter may be visible only momentarily; signals are increasingly disguised to merge into background noise.

Dr Withington notes the advantages drones bring to ESM. A lorry-mounted system with a ten-metre antenna can detect transmitters roughly 13km away. The same receiver on a drone at an altitude of 1,000 metres can see for 130km. Having antennae on drones is also more useful when an attack may come from any direction. It avoids blind spots caused by topography.

The Ukrainians are reluctant to discuss what they are up to. But not all their research is being done in-house. At Eurosatory, a European defence exhibition held in June, Aaronia, a German manufacturer, unveiled a SIGINT electronics package that can be mounted on a drone. The developers say three such drones working in tandem can pinpoint transmitters to within 25 metres from up to 75km away.

At 5kg, Aaronia’s product is inconveniently heavy. Sky Spy, based in Delaware, recently demonstrated Agent 001, a 500-gram electronics package that can be mounted on a small Orqa quadcopter. This proved able to detect, identify and locate “hostile” radios as part of an exercise in Estonia. Agent 001 also has on-board processing, linked to the drone’s camera, so it can move towards a transmitter and capture video for its operator to confirm the identity of the source.

One limitation of small drones, says Dr Withington, is that the amount of processing capacity they can carry is restricted. Such capacity is essential for sifting through signal data. Drone-control signals may, for example, be hidden in Wi-Fi.

New processors and AI software are, however, making small drones vastly more capable. One bit of kit that can be mounted onto a drone, known as Barn Owl, has been developed by NxGenComm of North Carolina. David Gross, NxGenComm’s marketing director, says Barn Owl follows all traffic in the Wi-Fi range, analysing changes to pick out the signatures of concealed military signals. He claims the process is fast enough to keep up with the most nimble frequency-hopping radios, and powerful enough to scan and analyse an 800MHz-wide swathe of radio signals.

Intelligence can go to commanders, or directly to other units. In one proposed set-up, a parliament of Barn Owls would be linked directly to interceptor drones. When they detected an incoming drone, they would launch an interceptor and guide it to the target’s location until it was close enough for visual confirmation by the operator. NxGenComm hopes to deploy Barn Owl to Ukraine in the next few months, and is in discussion with American military customers.

As well as locating enemy drones, ESM can also help identify their control frequencies so that they can be jammed. Both sides get round this by flying some drones via fibre-optic control cables, which unspool as they fly. Such drones, which can carry 50km of fibre, emit no radio signals. Similarly, some AI-enabled drones can operate incommunicado, flying and striking targets without operator input.

In the meantime, however, the vast majority of drones still rely on radio, and the electronic-warfare arms race continues. Falling behind can be disastrous: if an enemy can jam communications and knock drones out of the sky while remaining invisible, heavy losses are sure to result. ■

item.title: OpenAI 的数学方法站不住脚
item.description:
Science & technology

科学与技术 | 展示你的推导过程 2026年11月5日 10月29日，顶尖数学家齐聚伦敦皇家学会，讨论数学领域的未来。对于人工智能正在取得的进展，与会者兴奋不已，同时也夹杂着对2026年初那段美好旧时光的怀念——那时，人类主导的数学还是唯一的选择。许多与会者也批评了AI实验室处理其模型突破的方式。近几个月来，实验室向该领域投放了大量论文，这些论文几乎让人类无法理解，并且对新结果的细节秘而不宣。数学家们表示，这种保密性增加了无谓错误的风险，并可能制造出进步的假象。他们认为实验室并未兑现提高透明度的承诺。 以美国实验室OpenAI于10月26日宣布解决另外三个长期难题为例。第一个是Kakeya猜...
item.content:encoded:
OpenAI 的数学方法站不住脚

科学与技术 | 展示你的推导过程 2026年11月5日

10月29日，顶尖数学家齐聚伦敦皇家学会，讨论数学领域的未来。对于人工智能正在取得的进展，与会者兴奋不已，同时也夹杂着对2026年初那段美好旧时光的怀念——那时，人类主导的数学还是唯一的选择。许多与会者也批评了AI实验室处理其模型突破的方式。近几个月来，实验室向该领域投放了大量论文，这些论文几乎让人类无法理解，并且对新结果的细节秘而不宣。数学家们表示，这种保密性增加了无谓错误的风险，并可能制造出进步的假象。他们认为实验室并未兑现提高透明度的承诺。

以美国实验室OpenAI于10月26日宣布解决另外三个长期难题为例。第一个是Kakeya猜想的证明，该猜想与如何旋转一根无限细的针同时尽可能少地扫过面积有关。迄今为止，该猜想已被证明在三维及以下维度成立。OpenAI表示，其证明将其推广到了任意维度。第二个是对指数时间假设（ETH）的反驳，该假设对任何算法解决特定问题的速度设定了上限。长期以来，人们一直认为该假设为真，它对计算生物学到数据库管理等学科都有影响。OpenAI表示，证明该假设为假“重新开启了”关于此类任务能多快完成的问题。对于ETH和Kakeya猜想，该实验室都发布了AI的输出，以便专家们开始梳理这些结果的含义。然而，对于第三个结果，却笼罩上了一层保密的面纱。它涉及Yang-Mills存在性与质量缺口问题，这是七个被称为“千禧年大奖难题”的里程碑式谜题之一。该问题问的是，一个名为Yang-Mills理论的数学框架——它为物理学家对宇宙的理解奠定了基础——是否建立在坚实的数学基础之上（用数学行话来说，即是否“存在”）。对许多物理学家而言，这个问题无关紧要——该理论已经作出了与现实数据相符的预测，因此其真实性被视为理所当然。但数学家们更加挑剔。OpenAI称其模型证明了Yang-Mills理论存在。但该公司几乎没有透露其他信息。相反，它选择将AI长达1147页的证明保密，而由一个由五位物理学家组成的“指导委员会”决定如何处理。该委员会表示，在发布之前，他们“需要先说服自己这是正确的”。在那之前，以及在委员会之外的其他人也同样满意之前，他们的声明是否值得认真对待仍然存疑。

这些担忧并非理论上的。自从OpenAI于9月8日发布了Navier-Stokes问题——另一个千禧年大奖难题——的解决方案以来，数学家们一直在试图理解其推导过程。他们知道这个证明值得理解，因为它附带了一份逻辑严密的“证书”，即所谓的Lean形式化证明。如果翻译成Lean代码的证明运行无误，那就验证了该证明中不存在不一致之处。在10月6日在线发表的一项研究中，由剑桥大学的Anders Hansen带领的团队表明，该证明的Lean验证实际上与论文中写的内容并不对应。这个问题不太可能是致命的。Hansen博士认为Lean代码确实准确地反映了Navier-Stokes问题的一个解法，但其内容与随附论文有所不同。OpenAI则回应称，其模型有可能得出了两个不同的证明。任何在国外摸索过路的人都知道，蹩脚的翻译会造成误解。数学也是如此。如果AI实验室不检查证明的Lean代码与其背后的思路是否一致，就可能造成不必要的混乱。正如伦敦帝国理工学院的Lean专家Kevin Buzzard在皇家学会的演讲中所说，AI实验室只做了工作的一部分。■

item.content:encoded:
糙米真的比白米更健康吗？

科学 | 健康新知 2026年11月5日 大米提供了全球近五分之一的热量。但哪一种大米最健康呢？糙米在碾磨过程中去除了纤维状外层（即麸皮）和富含营养的胚芽后，就变成了白米，因此营养常识自然倾向于前者。事实上，一些引人注目的发现似乎也支持这种偏好。然而，仔细一看，大米的颜色可能并不是最重要的因素。

大米富含淀粉，消化后会转化为葡萄糖，也就是血糖。如果身体难以调节血糖，最终可能发展为2型糖尿病。来看看一项对八项观察性研究的综述，这些研究追踪了577,426人的饮食和健康状况。2022年发表在《BMJ Open》上的研究人员计算出，一旦每日食用量超过约两份158克的白米饭，每增加一份，患病风险就会增加13%。与此同时，糙米似乎具有一定的保护作用。麸皮中的纤维会减缓淀粉的分解，因此葡萄糖会更平缓地进入血液。麸皮和胚芽还含有镁、B族维生素和其他可能帮助身体调节血糖的营养素。2010年发表在《Archives of Internal Medicine》上的一篇论文（已纳入2022年的综述）分析了三项研究，这些研究对197,228名美国人进行了14至22年的跟踪。模型分析表明，每天用50克糙米替代50克白米饭，与2型糖尿病风险降低16%相关。

然而，相关性并不等于因果关系。偏好糙米的人往往吸烟更少、运动更多，整体饮食也更健康。尽管2022年和2010年论文的作者试图考虑这些混杂的生活方式差异，但他们承认其研究结果仍可能存在偏差。

那么，当研究人员真正指导人们吃糙米而不是白米时，会发生什么？效果不大。2022年的综述还考察了11项随机对照试验，涉及1,034名参与者。被分配吃糙米的人在短期或长期血糖控制方面没有显示出统计学上的显著改善。也没有明确证据表明胰岛素敏感性有所提高——胰岛素有助于细胞吸收葡萄糖。这些试验也未一致发现血压的改善。

事实证明，对血糖影响更大的不是大米的颜色，而是其中一种名为直链淀粉的淀粉含量。直链淀粉能够抵抗快速消化，从而限制血糖的急剧升高。2015年发表的一项对32项随机对照试验的综述指出，直链淀粉含量——这在很大程度上取决于水稻品种——是决定大米使血糖升高的剧烈程度的“最持续重要的”因素。加工方式也很重要。蒸谷米——即稻谷在碾磨前经过浸泡和蒸煮——会将B族维生素从麸皮转移到米粒中，同时使其淀粉更难被消化。2018年发表在《Nutrition》上的一项实验发现，在无糖尿病的人群中，食用蒸谷米而非普通白米，可使随后两小时内血糖的累计升高幅度降低38%。它似乎也优于普通糙米。

类似的技巧也可以在家中实现。将煮熟的米饭（无论是糙米还是白米）冷藏，会改变其中部分淀粉的结构，使其消化速度变慢。但需要注意：为限制细菌滋生，米饭应在一小时内冷却，并在一天内仅重新加热一次，加热至冒热气即可。■

想要一份免费、基于证据的健康指南吗？请订阅我们的每周《健康新知》通讯。

item.title: 不要孩子会传染吗？
item.description:
Culture

文化 | （别）做我的宝贝 2026年11月5日 一切都完了。在韩国，宠物婴儿车的销量已超过婴儿车。日本的寺庙有时为狗祈福的次数比为婴儿祈福还多。传统观念曾认为，当一对夫妇养了小狗，他们就会开始考虑为人父母——然后开始尝试怀孕。但越来越多的宠物“父母”将四条腿的动物视为两条腿后代的永久替代品。一些公司已经开始提供“宠物假”，以便员工能与新宠物增进感情或在宠物生病时照顾它。有些人觉得这一趋势毫无可爱之处。教皇方济各警告“人口寒冬”，并冷峻地谴责不生育的选择是“自私的”。埃隆·马斯克表示，出生率下降是“文明目前面临的最大危险”。按GDP计算的前15个国家——包括美国、中国和印度——现在都低于人口...
item.content:encoded:
不要孩子会传染吗？

文化 | （别）做我的宝贝 2026年11月5日 一切都完了。在韩国，宠物婴儿车的销量已超过婴儿车。日本的寺庙有时为狗祈福的次数比为婴儿祈福还多。传统观念曾认为，当一对夫妇养了小狗，他们就会开始考虑为人父母——然后开始尝试怀孕。但越来越多的宠物“父母”将四条腿的动物视为两条腿后代的永久替代品。一些公司已经开始提供“宠物假”，以便员工能与新宠物增进感情或在宠物生病时照顾它。有些人觉得这一趋势毫无可爱之处。教皇方济各警告“人口寒冬”，并冷峻地谴责不生育的选择是“自私的”。埃隆·马斯克表示，出生率下降是“文明目前面临的最大危险”。按GDP计算的前15个国家——包括美国、中国和印度——现在都低于人口更替水平。出生率下降可能导致世界人口在本世纪晚些时候出现自14世纪黑死病杀死数千万人以来的首次缩减。英国《金融时报》专栏作家卡米拉·卡文迪什女男爵给那些推迟生育或放弃生育的人起了个名字：“或许一代”。在一本引人入胜的新书中，她探讨了为什么“我们曾经认为最深刻的人类本能——传宗接代——正在衰退。”婴儿荒的后果显而易见：老龄化社会将不得不依赖更少的年轻人来推动增长、为养老金和公共服务提供资金。这些后果也是巨大的。出生率下降将重塑文化、社会与地缘政治。根据一些预测，到2050年，尼日利亚将超过美国成为第三人口大国（尽管此类估计备受争议）。卡文迪什女男爵提出，低增长国家可能相互入侵，以扩充本国人口并转移国内紧张与焦虑。她预测世界将变得不那么和平，而且可能更加宗教化，因为“地球上更大比例的人口将生活在以伊斯兰教或基督教人口为主的国家。”随着更多人选择只生一个孩子，这引发了“亲属崩溃”——兄弟姐妹和其他亲属减少。50年前，普通的35岁加拿大人大约有20个在世的堂表亲。今天，她大约有10个；到2095年，她可能只有5个。根据美国国家科学院发表的一项研究，到本世纪末，65岁人群在世亲属数量将比1950年减少38%。披头士乐队关于“所有孤独的人”的忧郁合唱或许正是未来将要发生的事。这股反向婴儿热的背后是什么？负担能力和住房成本受到广泛关注。当人们觉得自己像个长不大的孩子、只能和父母住在一起时，想要生孩子的人就更少了。多伦多大学的本杰明·库亚尔的一项研究估计，美国近年出生率下降中约一半可能归因于房价；如果房价保持稳定，1990年至2020年期间本应多出生约1300万婴儿。然而，即使在住房并非特别昂贵的国家（包括日本），生育率也大幅下降。机会成本可能是一个更大的因素。孩子需要大量时间。随着国家变得富裕，这些时间的替代用途变得更有吸引力。许多父母认为，如果把资源集中在给一两个孩子报汉语课和小提琴课上，而不是在三个或四个孩子之间分散资源，他们更有可能赢得教育军备竞赛。学者称之为“密集型”育儿；也有人用“直升机”和“虎妈”来类比。“社会传染”影响着人们对是否生育以及生几个孩子的看法，卡文迪什女男爵饶有趣味地指出。TikTok视频赞美光鲜的#无孩生活，显然包括午后小睡、遗愿清单旅行、大笔储蓄和提前退休。（抱歉，精疲力竭的父母们，后悔已经来不及了。）研究表明，电视节目——包括MTV的《16岁怀孕》和巴西讲述小家庭（尽管功能失调）的肥皂剧——也导致了生育率下降。越来越多的“痛苦回忆录”抱怨做父母和婚姻有多难，这同样起到了避孕套的作用。朋友和兄弟姐妹会强烈影响一个人想要几个孩子。例如，移居英国的波兰女性比留在国内的同胞生育更多孩子，“与她新国家的家庭平均水平保持一致，尽管在伦敦抚养孩子的成本往往高于华沙，”卡文迪什女男爵写道。那些认为自己可能喜欢孩子但在等待合适伴侣、合适时机、合适存款的人，可能被误导了。卡文迪什女男爵对试管婴儿和卵子冷冻提出了尖锐批评；诊所给女性描绘的为人父母前景比数据所支持的要乐观得多。冷冻胚胎的成功率差异很大，取决于女性年龄，但英国全国平均水平低于30%。男性随着年龄增长也面临鲜少被讨论的问题。一场“精子末日”正在悄然发生，许多国家的男性精子数量急剧下降，可能因为接触家居用品所致。年龄也会使精子质量下降，即使那些对生物钟滴答作响保持警觉的人也不一定把男性的生育力下降考虑在内。怎样才能让婴儿荒不再恶化？移民可以有所帮助，但往往不受欢迎，而且许多国家正在变得不那么欢迎移民。说服人们多生孩子几乎没有成功。宣传活动更可能适得其反而非惹人遐想。比如“为了丹麦做爱吧”电视广告（鼓励夫妇去度假并发送怀孕证明以赢取奖品），或新加坡的说唱（“我是爱国丈夫，你是爱国妻子，让我们履行公民义务，制造生命吧！”）。卡文迪什女男爵列举了11个不那么令人尴尬的催生点子，从明智的（让两性都更多了解生物钟）到不太可能的（重塑整个教育体系，让人们能更早成家）。有些是不言而喻的，比如努力让生育不再那么政治化和两极化。其他建议则令人费解：例如，有孩子的家庭是否应该拥有更多选票？已故人口学家兼经济学家保罗·德梅尼提议，父母应为其每个孩子获得一张代理投票权。这有助于抵消年长选民在投入更多医疗保健和更少教育方面的明显自利倾向。但这似乎不太可能成为政治外衣。归根结底，生育是带有公共后果的个人选择。紧迫的问题是，“或许一代”是否会变成“不要一代”。对此，人口学家和作家们只能等待下一章。■

item.title: What is it like to be a newborn?
item.description:
Culture

Culture | Born wild Nov 5th 2026 The naked creature in the incubator measures perhaps 50 centimetres and weighs some 900 grams. It scowls and twitches but cannot smile. Its skin is almost transparent, and its veins close to invisible; it will take a doctor several minutes first to find one and t...
item.content:encoded:
What is it like to be a newborn?

Culture | Born wild

Nov 5th 2026

The naked creature in the incubator measures perhaps 50 centimetres and weighs some 900 grams. It scowls and twitches but cannot smile. Its skin is almost transparent, and its veins close to invisible; it will take a doctor several minutes first to find one and then to draw a few drops of blood. It is probably intubated to help breathing; another tube trickles milk directly to the stomach. If you put tape on this fragile being, you will tear its skin. But if you leave it, it will cry.

Clémentine Goldszal, a French journalist, is consumed by this image and by a single imperative: to find out what birth is like for newborns, and how they experience the multiple medical interventions that may, in a worst case, immediately follow. She would interview them if she could. But of course there is no communication. When her own son Lucien was born, what she took as sweet kittenish sounds turned out to be signs of acute respiratory distress. An apparently lively baby may, in fact, be having convulsions.

She decided to “construct a phenomenology of the newborn” by spending many months as an observer in the neonatal unit of the Necker in Paris. This is a superb hospital, especially for its care of premature babies, rated seventh in the world. Sick babies are rushed there from all over France. Standing in a corner of the incubator rooms, out of the way, she sees nurses ceaselessly watching the beeping monitors, checking on breathing and feeding. In other rooms she watches operations so delicate, performed with miniature instruments, that a margin of error of a millimetre would be a catastrophe.

What she wanted to decipher was the attitude of medical staff to the newborn: whether or not they considered them fully human, individual and even having personalities. She had viewed Lucien as merely “a generic entity” for some weeks, and found it hard to say his name. But at Necker newborn patients were all called by their names and treated tenderly. They were assumed to have agency, if only to close their eyes or poo in their nappies. When those nappies were changed, blankets were put over the incubators to shield their privacy. After all, in French law, they were individuals as soon as they drew breath and no longer occupied their mother’s womb.

And yet without their consent, these babies were invaded. They were injected, intubated, placed among noisy machines and blinded by harsh lights. Tiny catheters were sent in to deliver fluids. In France 94% of babies born between 27 and 31 weeks left the hospital in perfect health. (At 25 weeks, though, the figure fell to 60%.)

These numbers were improving steadily, and had been doing so ever since the days when the only treatment for a struggling newborn was to dangle it by its heels or, in the case of Louis XIII of France, dose it with red wine. Nonetheless, Ms Goldszal worries about the long-term effects of brutal modern procedures, even wondering whether her disabled or confused friends were damaged by them, long before they knew how to complain.

She paints a gripping, vivid picture of life at Necker, especially the nurses, permanently exhausted but perceptive enough to lay a gentle hand on a newborn, turn down the lighting, or rock them. It is the medical setting, among people in scrubs and the tang of sanitiser, that thrills her: she finds herself surrounded at staff meetings by “an entire continent” of words she can’t understand: oesophageal atresia, hypocalcaemia, exomphalos.

Ms Goldszal goes only sketchily into the philosophy of personhood and the difficult legal line between the full-term fetus inside the womb and the newborn outside it. For ideas of ensoulment she has even less time. She envies religious Jews their belief that God breathes life into the fetus at the moment of birth, but she is a modern woman; this is really just “magical thinking”.

All she needs to know she has seen at Necker, and it is “fundamentally prosaic”: new life appears where before there was nothing, and medical ingenuity does its best to ensure that life does not swiftly return to nothing again.

Yet a mystery remains. The last epigram that opens the book comes from J.G. Ballard, an English writer, recording the birth of his daughter: “For the first few seconds I had the sense she was immensely old. She looked like something from Egyptian sculpture, streamlined by time. Within a few seconds she was suddenly very young.” Newborns may seem able to tell us nothing. But perhaps sometimes, for a moment, their eyes and their parents can. ■

item.title: What goes on behind the doors of Claridge’s?

item.content:encoded:
What goes on behind the doors of Claridge’s?

Culture | Fit for a king

Nov 5th 2026

THINGS CHANGE all the time inside hotels. Guests check in and out; towels and bed sheets are regularly laundered (or so you would hope). Hotels are also forced to accommodate upheavals that take place outside their doors. Two recent books, “The Finest Hotel in Kabul” and “Hotel Exile”, explored the turmoil of the 20th century from the front desks of hotels in Afghanistan and France. Now readers can journey to Claridge’s, one of London’s most prestigious hotels.

Martin Williams, a historian, traces how the hotel has witnessed all manner of political and cultural shifts since 1812. This is a top-down view of history, for Claridge’s clients have always been exceptionally posh. Princes and empresses slept there on visits to Britain; the future George IV, then prince regent, was thought to have slept there with lovers.

In periods of turmoil, such as the revolutions of 1848 and the second world war, European royals and aristocrats ousted from their countries took refuge in Mayfair. Alexander, the crown prince of Yugoslavia, was born in one of its suites in 1945. (Dirt was rumoured to have been spread under the bed so he could say he was born “on Yugoslavian soil”.) Legend holds that a diplomat once telephoned the hotel and asked to speak to the king. “Certainly, sir,” the operator said. “But which one?”

The war years are invariably the most fascinating. Soldiers back from Dunkirk—their uniforms still covered in “salt, sand and sweat”—lunched in the restaurant alongside women in hats. (Like the best hotels, this book pays attention to the details.) American officials moved in to be close to the embassy and were charmed by the hotel’s old-world grandeur. Though Dwight Eisenhower, then commander of American forces in Europe, was not among them: he took offence to his room’s “whorehouse pink” decor.

In the decades since, many notable people have strolled through the lobby. Audrey Hepburn first met William Wyler, the director of “Roman Holiday” (1953), in the hotel; the movie would make her a star and an Oscar winner. In 1974 Agatha Christie made one of her last public appearances at a dinner there, when she celebrated the premiere of the film adaptation of “Murder on the Orient Express”. In 1970 Jackie Kennedy Onassis prompted the hotel to overturn its long-standing policy banning women from wearing trousers.

The trousers tussle notwithstanding, Claridge’s has managed a difficult balance of tradition and innovation over the course of its two centuries. Mr Williams shows how it has adapted time and again to changing social mores and expectations of high-end hospitality. Today it lures foodies and fashionistas. Gordon Ramsay and Noma have had stints in the restaurant; since 2009 the hotel has invited a fashion designer to create its Christmas tree. (This year’s will be unveiled on November 25th, though the designer has yet to be announced.) If you do not feel like shelling out between £1,500 and £60,000 ($2,000-80,000) for a suite, “Claridge’s” offers a sweet (and cheap) escape. ■

item.title: Is it time to end the era of remote work?
item.description:
Culture

Culture | In praise of watercoolers Nov 5th 2026 Those mulling the current AI boom should look back to a kitchen in Google’s office in the early 2000s. Two employees, Noam Shazeer and Georges Harik, began to chat about how computers differentiated between essential and superfluous information. T...
item.content:encoded:
Is it time to end the era of remote work?

Culture | In praise of watercoolers

Nov 5th 2026

Those mulling the current AI boom should look back to a kitchen in Google’s office in the early 2000s. Two employees, Noam Shazeer and Georges Harik, began to chat about how computers differentiated between essential and superfluous information. This chance encounter windingly led to the mechanism that underpins large language models.

Had Google allowed remote work, Mr Shazeer and Mr Harik might never have spoken. In-person spitballing has led to ideas ranging from the hugely consequential (IBM’s personal computer) to the hugely entertaining (“Finding Nemo”). That is one reason why bosses often lament the rise of remote work, notes a new book by Natalia Emanuel and Emma Harrington, two economists. In 2019 American workers spent 7% of their paid days working at home. Now it is about a quarter.

Studies suggest that remote work may increase the quantity of output while decreasing its quality. In 2025 a review of return-to-office mandates at large banks found that when firms called analysts back to the office for a few days each week, the accuracy of their earnings forecasts leaped 15% compared with peers at banks that remained fully remote.

What is more, remote work tends to dent the sort of tasks that rarely show up in measures of output. Senior software engineers write more code from the comfort of their homes, but they review junior employees’ work less comprehensively. Lost mentorship and undiscovered ideas can affect the future of a firm.

Such losses may be why the shift has stung new graduates in particular. A new study by Peter John Lambert of the London School of Economics and Yannick Schindler of the University of Oxford suggests remote work, not AI, is to blame for young jobseekers’ woes of late. Jobs done entirely online tend to be susceptible to being done remotely. Firms that are reluctant to let untested employees work away from their boss’s watchful eye may be choosing not to hire them at all.

So why not cancel the corporate Zoom subscription and squeeze back into the cubicle? The authors note that some employees are well-served by remote work: for example, parents and people with disabilities. For most companies a mix is best. To help bosses settle on the right number of days in-office, “In Person” features a “calculator” that asks them to add and subtract days based on the firm’s characteristics. But what executive would not say the stakes of their business are high (add two days), or that innovation is crucial to their firm’s future (add three days)? When it comes to such decisions, psychologists may be more helpful than economists.

Still, many of the book’s points are well-taken. How many days employees spend at the office may be less important than whether they overlap with key colleagues. Hot-desking is a scourge, as would-be collaborators sit together only occasionally. And if bosses want to reap the benefits of in-person culture, they also need to show face. “In Person” should contribute to an ongoing conversation about why remote work has remained so persistent if it comes with so many drawbacks. Watercooler-chat lovers, rejoice. ■

item.content:encoded:
中国技术帮助专制的非洲政府镇压异议

文化 | 更大的老大哥 2026年11月5日 当中国斥资2亿美元为位于亚的斯亚贝巴的非洲联盟（AU）建造新总部时（如图），这被视为一种慷慨之举。但五年后，技术人员注意到了奇怪的事情。每天深夜，由中国提供的服务器都会疯狂地嗡嗡作响。数据正被导出到上海的服务器，其中包括机密电子邮件、外交官备忘录、监控摄像头录像等等。据称，后来对大楼进行清扫的阿尔及利亚和埃塞俄比亚专家在桌子底下和墙壁内发现了麦克风。中国政府及相关企业华为和中兴均否认有任何不当行为。这并不意外。更令人沮丧的是非洲领导人的公开反应，他们愤怒的对象不是监控行为，而是帮助曝光此事的记者。英国记者保罗·肯扬在一本扣人心弦的新书中指出，中国是最新一个既榨取非洲大陆又扶植腐败地方权势人物外部势力。他更广泛的警告是，非洲大部分地区正在被中国科技接管。许多专制政府正在使用中国系统来监控其人民，尤其是异见人士。例如，这意味着通过中国公司安装的移动电话网络进行窥探。不妨想象一下，新疆的信息控制手段正被应用于津巴布韦、肯尼亚及其他地方。肯扬先生对细节有敏锐的洞察力，但倾向于夸大其词，他声称在非洲的中国工程师是“中国数字殖民主义的步兵，使极权政权得以在非洲繁荣，因为中国希望如此”。中国的科技正迅速遍及非洲，部分原因在于慷慨的贷款使其成本低廉。其中许多技术被用于阻碍言论自由和上网自由。例如，中国公司Geedge出口中国“防火墙”的版本，以便非洲政府可以尝试审查公民在网上看到的内容。恶劣的政权最热衷于向中国学习。在乌干达丘陵起伏的首都坎帕拉，竖起了白色杆子；杆顶装有约5000个摄像头，将图像传输到83个监控中心。这被向公众展示为降低犯罪率的措施：监控人员使用人工智能、面部识别和生物特征分析来追踪个人。但它也是专制政府的工具：总统约韦里·穆塞韦尼可以监控那些支持反对派的人。多年来，美国、英国和其他富裕国家一直以安全风险为由回避与华为和中兴的合同。在非洲则没有这样的犹豫，那里很少有政府能承受得起损害与一个重要贸易伙伴关系的风险。中国还为阿尔及利亚和尼日利亚等国提供了贷款，以支付其建造和发射的卫星费用。在信息争夺的相关领域，肯扬先生指出，越来越多的中国通讯人员——他称之为“宣传员”——正在非洲设立据点。中国官方通讯社新华社在非洲大陆设有约35个分社，超过任何其他新闻机构。最终目标是什么？中国正在获取非洲的自然资源，包括其丰富的石油储量和稀土。但它也在试图为其对西方价值观的挑战赢得政治支持。中国可能成功地在非洲制造一个“分裂网”，使数字互动只发生在严密监控的空间内。肯扬先生认为，这将是一个没有异议的“无菌世界”。这也将标志着与现状的改变——如今，为了压制反对声音，政府有时会让数百万人断网数月甚至数年。“中国的非洲帝国”是一个清醒的警告：正如非洲联盟总部大楼那样，中国未必是它所声称的那种良善伙伴。有时候，你需要对礼物仔细审视。■

item.description:

item.content:encoded:
Explaining the popularity of Max Richter’s compositions

Culture | A sonic sweet spot

Nov 5th 2026

DOES ANY musician get around as much as Max Richter? In April he will be in Las Vegas, providing musical direction for Oprah Winfrey’s “immersive symphony of senses” at the Sphere. He is on screens: his soundtrack for “Hamnet” was nominated for an Academy Award this year. And he may well be in your bedroom: “Sleep”, his eight-and-a-half-hour-long composition, has been streamed more than 2bn times.

But it is probably through “On the Nature of Daylight”, a soulful six-minute composition for string quintet from 2004, that Mr Richter (pictured) has most successfully colonised the consciousness of listeners. It heightens emotions in at least a dozen films and television programmes, including “My Brilliant Friend” and “Arrival”. It transforms millions of commutes into occasions for reverie. Listeners will hear echoes of it on “While the Flood Rages”, a new album.

Achieving such ubiquity would be a feat for any composer. That Mr Richter writes classical music makes it more remarkable. Born in Germany and brought up in Britain, Mr Richter studied at the Royal Academy of Music in London and with Luciano Berio, an Italian modernist. If you do not detect the classical pedigree in Mr Richter’s music, he may point it out to you. In an interview at his studio in the Cotswolds he relocates from the sofa to the piano to demonstrate that a falling sequence of notes from his new album is reminiscent of the music of Johann Sebastian Bach. His record label is Decca, among the most storied in classical music.

But the genre would confine Mr Richter if he did not bend it. Kraftwerk, a German electronic band, is an influence alongside American minimalists such as Philip Glass. The piano in his studio keeps company with banks of vintage synthesisers, giving it the appearance of “mission control”, he jokes. As is fashionable, he deems the conventional distinction between classical music and other sorts to be “bizarre”.

Mr Richter’s medley of influences and instincts have landed him in a musical sweet spot shared with few contemporary composers. Thanks in part to his classical chops, he collaborates with choreographers as well as film directors. “While the Flood Rages” draws from music he wrote for a ballet, “MaddAddam”, which in turn is inspired by a post-apocalyptic trilogy by Margaret Atwood, teller of “The Handmaid’s Tale”. In April the Orchestre de Paris will play the premiere of a cello concerto Mr Richter is writing.

His music has an emotional directness that gives it much wider appeal than that of most living classical composers. Mari Samuelsen, a Norwegian violinist who often performs it, finds it “extremely meditative and cleansing”, both “simple and complex at the same time”. Although film and phone are its natural habitat, Mr Richter’s music also packs concert halls. Audiences tend to be younger than at conventional classical concerts, she says, and more prone to share reactions on social media.

To some listeners the sweet spot is too sweet. Some think his partnerships with brands such as Krug champagne and Christian Dior, a fashion house, are evidence that his art lulls rather than challenges. Alex Ross, a prominent critic, has written that Mr Richter’s pieces “exude a gentle fatalism, a numbed acquiescence” even in the face of “global disaster”. Many deal explicitly with political themes. “Voices”, from 2020, incorporates text from the UN human-rights declaration. “Sleep”, Mr Richter has said, is a “protest” against a “very super-industrialised, intense, mechanised way of living”. “Daylight” comes from an album that opposes America’s war in Iraq. Yet most of the time the strife seems to be happening in the distance.

“While the Flood Rages” considers the aftermath of apocalypse, environmental vandalism and corporate greed. Mr Richter says the music is “more highly coloured” than what he normally composes, echoing the “stylistic omnivorousness” of Ms Atwood’s writing. Synthetic and recorded sounds—of water, of gunfire—suggest a world made strange and threatening. But Mr Richter’s sensibility has the last word. Piano, strings and a church-like choir, sometimes in counterpoint with eerier music, seem to suggest that something good will prevail. The listener, unsettled at first by the album’s dystopian theme, may come away consoled.

That is often the effect of Mr Richter’s music. Rather than depict evil, he imagines alternatives to it. “We’re flooded with negativity, with negative images and negative storytelling,” largely because of social media, he says. “I’m looking to celebrate and elevate the things that are not that, which are ordinary…human qualities which have been with us for ever and will continue to be with us, but are easy to overlook.” While floods rage, Mr Richter offers audiences a life raft. No wonder he’s so in demand. ■

Correction (November 5th 2026): An earlier version of this story said that “On the Nature of Daylight” could be heard in “Black Mirror”. That was incorrect. Sorry.

多洛雷斯·韦尔塔为农场工人权利而战——却深藏惊人秘密

讣告 | 讣告 | 真相与权力 2026年11月5日 1986年11月下旬，美国农场工人联合会（UFW）这个工会组织正准备庆祝。当月早些时候，时任总统罗纳德·里根签署了《移民改革与控制法》，这是UFW花费数月游说的成果。该法案为长期居住在美国的无证移民提供了获得公民身份的途径，并给予能够证明受雇满90天的农场工人合法永久居留权。法案还处罚了故意雇佣无证工人的雇主——工会担心这些工人会拉低工资，并在罢工期间充当工贼。就在为庆祝这一立法胜利而召开新闻发布会前不久，UFW的创始人之一塞萨尔·查韦斯告诉另一位创始人多洛雷斯·韦尔塔，她需要去一趟佛罗里达。他说，出了危机。所以她当然去了，因为这就是她一贯的作风：哪里有工人需要她，她就去哪里。但当她到达佛罗里达时，发现根本没有危机。没有人期待她的到来。“他们只是想把我支开，这样他们就可以把功劳揽在自己身上，”她后来说。“典型的男性沙文主义把戏。”但这并不罕见，正如一位活动家同事所回忆的那样：“人们默认[查韦斯]是领袖，而多洛雷斯是运动的管家。”事实上，他们是一起创立了这个工会——只是与他不同，她还得在工作的同时抚养14个孩子。他有着深情的深色眼睛、亲切交谈的风格和对麦克风的热爱，是魅力四射的台前人物。但她是工会的首席谈判代表。他可以发表演讲；但还有抵制活动需要组织，合同需要谈判，还有需要帮助的人。她的母亲艾丽西亚也有同样顽强务实的性格。离婚后，艾丽西亚带着三个孩子从新墨西哥州来到加利福尼亚州中央谷地的斯托克顿——这里是加州农业的心脏地带。在做过女招待、罐头厂工人和餐馆老板之后，艾丽西亚经营了一家拥有70间客房的酒店，欢迎移民工人入住，常常在房费过高时予以免除。多洛雷斯回忆说，艾丽西亚“把自己当成他们的母亲”，给他们规定宵禁时间，确保他们把挣的钱寄回家而不是酗酒花光，还邀请他们参加舞会，让他们认识好姑娘并安定下来——很多人也确实如此。艾丽西亚曾参加1938年的罐头厂工人罢工，并加入斯托克顿的公民团体。多洛雷斯从她身上学到了行动主义——无非就是帮助那些需要帮助的人，为那些无法自我发声的人呐喊。在接受教师培训后，她在20多岁时转向全职组织工作，加入了斯托克顿的社区服务组织。该组织的创始人把她介绍给了查韦斯，很快两人共同创立了这个组织——在与另一个农场工人组织合并后，它成为UFW。从一开始，她就毫不逊色。作为一位“经验丰富的说客”，她在给查韦斯的信中写道：“我能够与其他说客进行平起平坐的对话。”民选官员开始怕她。一位加州州参议员回忆说，她“不知疲倦”且“不循常规”。“多洛雷斯会带来几百人，他们就堵在你办公室门外。”虽然睡在参议院走廊里听起来很不舒服，但比起她工会成员们所习惯的境遇，这根本不算什么。他们在田地里每天工作16个小时。没有厕所：女工只能蹲在毛巾或毯子后面。唯一的饮用水整天放在太阳下暴晒的水箱里。没有医疗保险或失业保险，如果农场主欺骗他们，他们也毫无申诉途径。于是她和查韦斯开始行动起来。1965年，他们这个以墨西哥农场工人为主的工会，加入了在加州德拉诺附近葡萄园罢工的2000名菲律宾工人。农场主雇佣工贼并拒绝谈判，以为可以像以前一样迫使工人退缩。但时代在变。罢工者得到了包括罗伯特·F·肯尼迪和马丁·路德·金在内的民权活动人士的支持。他们借鉴民权运动的策略，呼吁抵制鲜食葡萄。到1970年，农场主们让步了，同意提高工资并承认工会。UFW的成员人数激增，五年后加州通过了一项法律，保护农场工人组织工会的权利，并让移民工人有资格获得医疗保险和其他福利。查韦斯成了英雄，加州及其他地区以他的名字命名街道、公园和学校，尽管有人私下议论他的威权倾向、对个人忠诚和顺从的执念。她则继续做工作，为女性权利奔走，鼓励她们竞选公职，参加纠察和抗议。年龄几乎没有让她放慢脚步；快60岁时，她在一次示威中被警察打断了肋骨，脾脏破裂。但直到今年，多洛雷斯才揭露了她最深的秘密：1993年去世的查韦斯曾在1966年强奸了她。他早在多年前就强迫她发生性关系。她的两个孩子是他的。她从未开口，因为“我不想伤害这场运动”。《纽约时报》的一项调查发现，他性侵和猥亵了多名女性及女孩，有些人年仅12岁。性别歧视渗透了他的工会。UFW组织者莉兹·沙利文在一次组织会议后被两名男子强奸，她回忆说，工会成员斥责她和那些公开谈论女性所受待遇的女同事。男性高层对“妇女解放和那些狗屁”毫无耐心。近几个月来，查韦斯的雕像被拆除，公园被改名。也有人指责多洛雷斯保持沉默，并 dismissing 她们关于遭受同事性骚扰和性侵的投诉。沙利文女士则持更宽容的看法。她敦促人们“把她看作一个有血有肉的人，有她的美好，也有她的缺点，就像我们所有人一样”。■

item.content:encoded:
政治

本周世界 2026年10月29日 以色列选举未产生明确的获胜者。在超过90%的选票清点完毕后，本雅明·内塔尼亚胡的阵营赢得了议会120个席位中的53席。反对党拿下67席，足以组成多数。但其中19席由阿拉伯政党获得，创下历史新高，而多数犹太反对党拒绝将其纳入执政联盟。一旦结果最终确定，联盟谈判将开始。选举前，内塔尼亚胡下令以军进入希伯伦——一处位于被占领的约旦河西岸的城市，此前巴勒斯坦枪手袭击一处军事检查站，造成两名士兵死亡。数千名巴勒斯坦人被迫离开家园，或房屋被拆除。来自巴基斯坦、沙特阿拉伯和土耳其——新麦加公约的三个签署国——的官员前往德黑兰，会晤伊朗安全负责人和总统。此次会晤举行之际，胡塞武装——伊朗支持的也门叛军——对沙特基础设施发动更多袭击，同时美国和以色列进一步打击伊朗的威胁日益加剧。未宣布任何突破性进展。约旦一场基督教葬礼上有九人被枪杀。该国空军对叙利亚境内的“恐怖组织”进行了回击。苏丹达尔富尔地区由叛军快速支援部队控制的尼亚拉市，一处市场遭军方无人机袭击，至少100人死亡，数十人受伤。据联合国统计，10月前三个星期内，无人机袭击已造成300多人死亡、数百人受伤。另外，快速支援部队的无人机袭击摧毁了政府军控制区的几座发电厂，导致大范围停电。数十个非洲代表团前往莫斯科出席与弗拉基米尔·普京的峰会。普京正试图将俄罗斯宣传为非洲国家比“殖民主义”西方更可靠的伙伴。坦桑尼亚一名反对派活动人士在内罗毕附近遭绑架，这是肯尼亚首都不再是地区异见人士避风港的最新迹象。特瓦哈·姆瓦伊帕亚是第三位在肯尼亚被绑架的坦桑尼亚知名异见人士，这似乎是一种令人担忧的趋势：东非各国政府串通镇压异见。朝鲜独裁者金正恩出人意料地访问了中国丹东。金正恩乘车通过一座跨越鸭绿江的桥梁抵达这座边境城市。其行程的官方理由是纪念中国在朝鲜战争期间对朝鲜的支持。外界纷纷猜测，他也可能是在与中方磋商，为可能同唐纳德·特朗普的会面做准备。在非军事区最近发生多起事件——包括一起造成三名韩国士兵受伤的地雷爆炸——之后，韩国提议与朝鲜就边境划界问题进行会谈。朝鲜是否接受该提议尚不清楚。爆炸发生后，朝鲜恢复了沿边境的广播，通过扬声器向韩国一侧播放宣传内容。西班牙马德里至塞维利亚线路上两列高速列车相撞，造成至少68人死亡。其中一列列车据报因计算机系统故障而停在轨道上。这起事故引发了对该国铁路维护的更多担忧。今年1月，在西班牙南部曾发生一列火车脱轨、另一列撞上其车厢的事故，导致46人死亡。法国全国又有超过1400人因抗议活动被捕，抗议伴随打砸和抢劫，但激烈程度不及前一个周末。示威前一天，一名39岁男子在巴黎附近从车内开枪，一名黑人男子中弹身亡，另有七人受伤，其中包括一名儿童。埃马纽埃尔·马克龙称之为“种族主义、恐怖主义袭击”。极右翼民粹主义者、明年总统选举的领跑者玛丽娜·勒庞正式启动竞选活动。她在与圣女贞德密切相关的城市奥尔良发表了首次竞选演讲。同一周末，她领导的国民联盟在党代会上再次选举乔丹·巴尔代拉为党主席。勒庞确认，如果该党执政，她将任命他为总理。乌克兰实施一项为期六天的停火，以便向俄罗斯占领的奥列什基市运送人道主义援助物资。据报道，停火范围扩展至赫尔松地区。与此同时，弗拉基米尔·普京与芬兰和挪威领导人通电话，为即将在阿布扎比举行的俄罗斯、乌克兰、美国三方会谈做准备。自2014年以来一直担任塞尔维亚总理或总统的亚历山大·武契奇在议会选举中承认败选。武契奇此前在学生领导的反腐败和反政府权力滥用的抗议活动持续两年后提前举行大选。数万人走上街头庆祝学生名单的惊人胜利。该名单由学生团体推选的候选人组成；学生们本人则不参选。俄罗斯如今在欧洲失去了两个关键盟友：塞尔维亚的武契奇和匈牙利的欧尔班·维克托。两名英国公民因与英国皇家空军费尔福德基地事件有关而被起诉，该事件被认为由伊朗指使。阴谋细节尚不清楚，但情报警告称伊朗正计划袭击该空军基地，促使美国撤出了其轰炸机机队。 路易斯·伊纳西奥·卢拉·达席尔瓦在巴西总统决选中再次当选，赢得52%的选票。这是首次出现第一轮排名第二的候选人赢得决选的情况。其保守派挑战者、首轮获胜者弗拉维奥·博索纳罗称这一结果“无法解释”，并暗示存在舞弊行为，但他的政党接受了结果。选举后，博索纳罗离开巴西前往迈阿密，违抗了法官要求他在既有刑事调查继续期间留在国内的命令。他在社交媒体帖子中表示，选举被“罪犯”窃取，这些“罪犯”建立了“暴政”。玛丽亚·科里纳·马查多返回委内瑞拉。这位反对派领导人十个月前离开该国去领取诺贝尔和平奖。自1月美国特种部队逮捕尼古拉斯·马杜罗以来，她已多次尝试回国。马查多呼吁重新举行选举，尽管她的政党被排除在特朗普政府斡旋的关于未来选举进程的谈判之外。美国国务卿马尔科·卢比奥表示，谈判正在取得进展，没有人应该试图“破坏这一进程”。加拿大反对党保守党在不列颠哥伦比亚省赢得了近100年来的首次选举。该省自2017年以来一直由左翼新民主党执政。保守党承诺削减繁文缛节，取消温室气体排放限制。他们还承诺提高不列颠哥伦比亚省的液化天然气产量，并支持新建一条从阿尔伯塔省到西海岸的石油管道。该党亲能源的议程必将面临法律挑战。查尔斯国王开始加勒比之行，该地区一些国家呼吁英国为奴隶制支付赔偿。多个政府希望这一问题在国王将出席的英联邦政府首脑会议上被列为重要议程，会议将在安提瓜和巴布达举行。

item.content:encoded:
商业

本周要闻 2026年10月29日

Anthropic发布了外界期待已久的IPO招股说明书，这有望成为有史以来规模最大的IPO之一，如果不是最大的话。其营收从2025年第二季度的7.87亿美元飙升至今年同期的116亿美元。其人事支出（包括基于股票的薪酬）从3.2亿美元增至近19亿美元。Anthropic报告本季度净亏损663亿美元，主要原因是与可转换为股票的债务公允价值重新评估相关的会计费用。实际上，它在第二季度实现了9.74亿美元的营业利润，而前三个月则录得近17亿美元的营业亏损。Anthropic的股市首秀可能发生在11月。

人工智能领域公布了更多融资交易。随着科技公司日益转向华尔街和资本市场为其投资提供资金，博通正在与美国银行及其他金融机构共同设立一个630亿美元的特别目的实体（SPV）。该SPV将购买博通的芯片和网络设备，并将其租赁给Anthropic。Meta通过股票发行筹集了375亿美元。它还计划从明年开始，通过定期出售新发行股票筹集至多600亿美元。Alphabet的股价下跌，因为其现金消耗速度远高于市场预期。微软的股价表现较好，因为其报告的资本支出低于华尔街预期，主要原因在于新数据中心的建设出现延迟。为了控制成本，微软希望通过一项“自愿离职计划”裁减6万名员工，占其全球员工总数的四分之一，该计划将给“可能正在考虑公司外部未来”的员工“一个新的选择，以实现这一转变”。Skydance在收购华纳兄弟后，也向员工提供了一项“自愿买断”计划，作为其削减成本努力的一部分。它告诉留任员工，从现在起他们必须每周五天到办公室工作，因为“在像我们这样的创意公司，最好的想法来自同一间屋子里的人”。

英国政府公布了预算，这是安迪·伯纳姆担任首相、约翰·希利担任财政大臣以来的首份预算。其中，预算将银行公司税附加税从3%提高至6%，为期15个月，以帮助支付家庭能源补贴。企业将从房产税的冻结或削减中受益，这意味着所有零售、酒店和休闲物业中将有一半完全不需要缴纳房产税。从2028年起，市长和地方当局将有权征收旅游税。政府还承诺到2030年将国防支出占GDP的3%作为目标，但将如何为此提供资金的细节留给了明年的支出审查。

克里斯蒂娜·拉加德宣布，她将于2月卸任欧洲央行行长一职，比其任期正式结束提前了九个月。拉加德于2019年成为欧洲央行行长，她原本没想到会在这个职位上待这么久，但她表示自己离开时“带着工作圆满完成的感觉”。她一直在与世界济论坛讨论可能担任其主席一事。欧洲理事会将任命她在欧洲央行的继任者，目前来自荷兰和西班牙的候选人领先。与此同时，欧洲央行管理委员会在法兰克福召开会议时并未对利率做出任何调整。美联储在最近一次会议上也维持利率不变，将基准利率维持在3.75%至4%的区间。美联储主席凯文·沃什承诺将继续施以“新的货币药方”以控制通胀。市场认为美联储将在未来几个月内加息。

美国经济第三季度年化增长率为3.4%，高于第二季度的2.2%。在这些数据公布之前，沃什指出经济增长已经走强，并称消费者支出和资本支出“健康”。JIO Platforms的IPO取得成功，筹集了31亿美元。这家印度电信公司的股价在首个交易日上涨27%，市值达到1370亿美元。Jio将利用所得资金偿还债务，同时进一步推进其在人工智能和卫星宽带领域的雄心。

波音股价大幅下跌，此前该公司确认将无法实现今年737飞机的生产和交付目标。其商用飞机部门报告季度营业亏损6.97亿美元，高于分析师预期，但国防、太空与安全业务利润飙升至4.92亿美元。奥迪宣布将在佐治亚州投资40亿美元建厂，这是其在美国的首家工厂。该工厂每年将生产20万辆运动型多用途车，创造4500个就业岗位，尽管奥迪母公司大众汽车正在裁减10万个工作岗位。奥迪首席执行官格诺特·多尔纳与唐纳德·特朗普在佐治亚州的一场竞选集会上共同宣布了这一消息。总统表示，如果没有关税，奥迪的决定就不会发生：在美国制造的欧洲汽车免征这些关税。

汽车行业向高科技聚焦的演变，体现在通用汽车决定将股票上市地从纽约证券交易所转至纳斯达克。通用汽车表示，纳斯达克是其“技术驱动战略”的自然归宿。该公司最近强调，它正在“利用前沿人工智能和机器学习突破来加速”自动驾驶领域的“开发”。

item.title: The Americans changing politics for the better
item.description:
Leaders

Leaders | The midterm elections Oct 29th 2026 MIDTERM ELECTIONS are always a referendum on the sitting American president, but rarely has an incumbent so wilfully put himself in the spotlight in defiance of his own unpopularity. As the campaign ends, Donald Trump is commandeering rallies in Repu...
item.content:encoded:
The Americans changing politics for the better

Leaders | The midterm elections

Oct 29th 2026

MIDTERM ELECTIONS are always a referendum on the sitting American president, but rarely has an incumbent so wilfully put himself in the spotlight in defiance of his own unpopularity. As the campaign ends, Donald Trump is commandeering rallies in Republican strongholds, a sign of his party’s vulnerability and his unwavering faith in his own star power. Away from the spotlight, however, something more surprising—and more important—has been happening: Hispanics and Asians have emerged as America’s most valuable voters.

The curse of American politics is its bitter partisanship. As voters have sorted themselves along racial, educational and geographical lines, the parties have spent less time trying to win converts from the other side and more whipping their own supporters into a permanent frenzy: 70% of Republicans are hostile towards Democrats and more than 80% of Democrats return the favour. The result is a style of politics that tugs public life towards the extremes, punishes compromise and puts getting people angry above getting things done.

Hispanic and Asian-American voters offer the best hope of arresting this baleful trend. They have become America’s crucial swing voters, with an outsize impact on races across the country. Compared with other blocs, their numbers are growing faster, their ideology is more fluid and their priorities are less divisive. That means they are likely to be good for America not just in these midterms, but also for many elections to come.

The biggest force on November 3rd will be Mr Trump’s unpopularity. His national net-approval rating stands at -27 points. The president is predicting victory in “record numbers”, but our forecast model suggests Democrats have a 95% chance of winning back the House and a 54% chance of taking the Senate. Polling puts Mr Trump underwater on every policy, from inflation to immigration. His great vulnerability is that voters blame higher bills on his fondness for tariffs and his choice to go to war with Iran.

The backlash has created openings for Democrats in states such as Kansas and Iowa, where even contemplating a blue victory would once have got Republican strategists sacked. Disenchanted rural voters who chose Mr Trump in 2024 may stay at home this time, as a protest against high diesel prices and poor markets for their crops. Polls say Democrats are winning back the young and peeling off working-class whites.

It would be good for America to have more battleground states. If Democrats win in places like Kansas and Texas, the power of incumbency could make them competitive in future elections, too. No group captures the potential for opening up politics as much as Hispanics and Asian-Americans.

One reason is demography. They are a growing fraction of the population—especially Hispanics, who are three times more numerous than Asian-Americans. Since 2006 their combined share of the electorate has increased by nine percentage points, to reach 21%. They are also highly diverse. The grandchildren of an immigrant from Ho Chi Minh City have a different outlook from a new arrival from Bangalore. Neither fits neatly into the familiar Democrat-Republican template.

And they are more likely to switch their votes. In 2012 Democrats thought they had a lock on Latinos and Asians. In 2024 the story was how they were becoming Trumpian. It has now become clear that they were swing voters all along.

White voters changed little between 2020 and 2024, while both Latinos and Asians lurched hard to the right. They were then the fastest to turn against Mr Trump in early 2025. The margin of support for Democrats has risen by 17 points among Latinos and 14 among Asians since 2024, compared with ten for whites and five for black voters. They are likely to help decide House races from suburban New York to Florida as well as Senate contests in Alaska, Kansas and Texas.

Part of the explanation for this is that these voters are the epitome of striving Americans who want to work hard and get ahead. Higher prices for food and fuel hit Hispanic voters particularly hard; housing costs affected Asian voters. Latinos are more than twice as likely to start businesses as white voters. Asians are likely to spend more time in education.

Many are recent arrivals or the children of immigrants, so their opinions have not yet hardened along party lines. In contrast to the rest of the voting population, if Hispanics and Asians hold one left-leaning position, they will not necessarily endorse others. Likewise, wanting a secure southern border does not equate to support for the hardline enforcement that has frightened Hispanic employees into staying away from work.

Instead, many are moderate. They have little truck with culture wars or polarisation. The economic policies they care about diverge from the tribal messages the parties use to stir up their bases. Whereas policies on abortion and trans rights are set at the extremes, economic management is suited to the swing voter’s pragmatic preference for the common good.

Almost anything that gives the parties a reason to appeal to the centre will benefit America, especially when it involves the virtues of hard work and prosperity. Democrats will need a winning economic message and a coherent plan for immigration. Republicans should reject their ferocious deportations and the ugly ultranationalism that denigrates Hispanic and Asian citizens for not being “heritage Americans”.

All Americans should therefore welcome these new swing voters. Thanks to them, fewer elections will be decided by hard-core party members in primaries, and more by the average voter in the general election. If politicians win more credit by accomplishing something in government, they will perhaps spend less of their time demonising the other side. If the economy seems to matter more and culture wars less, America will be more prosperous and better governed. Hispanic and Asian immigrants want the chance to thrive. Their votes will help ensure America thrives with them. ■
